item.title: Investigating Ephemeral Supply Chain Tampering
item.description:
UNC7017 hijacked AOMEI Technology's update pipeline using five-to-ten-minute tampering windows to deliver the CROSSROAD downloader and SHINYROAD backdoor, hitting IT, telecom, and education sectors across twelve countries between April and July 2026.
Key details:
- The core innovation here is ephemeral configuration tampering. UNC7017 modified two AOMEI update config files (down_html.ini and Notifycfg.ini) on the vendor's origin servers for windows as short as five minutes (May 28: 10 min, July 16: 6 min, July 20: 5 min), then reverted both files to authentic content. CROSSROAD itself reinforced this anti-forensic loop: the loader parsed the local copy of down_html.ini and restored the version field (thrid) back to 5 and the download URL back to the legitimate www2.aomeisoftware[.]com domain before deleting itself using an alternate data stream rename trick (renaming the primary :$DATA stream to :wtfbbq then unlinking via FileDispositionInfo). Analysts checking the vendor URL hours after an alert fires see only clean files, making detections look like false positives. Endpoint-cached copies in %PROGRAMFILES(X86)%\AOMEI\*\Tmphtml\ are the authoritative forensic record.
- The delivery chain used Notifycfg.ini as an execution trigger. On July 16, UNC7017 injected over 35,000 lines of dummy configuration sections into Notifycfg.ini (SHA256: d2f9ef2429312667f0512504b6a19ba4a9cc5514f1b2933923dd42f75a1c5934) to override client version checks and force immediate execution of upgrade-now.exe from the local html/ directory. On July 20, a separate Notifycfg.ini modification added an invisible 1x1 pixel popup (Priority=9999) pointing to file://8.210.84[.]56/DavWWWRoot/campaign/24hour-flash-sale.html, silently coercing NetNTLMv2 hashes to an actor-controlled IP via WebDAV. Block outbound SMB (TCP 445) and WebDAV to external IPs; this vector harvests credentials even when binary execution is blocked.
- CROSSROAD (upgrade-now.exe, SHA256: 9a58e8f49edf5644e5728f74cf36f560d3d486fa51db4db69d927963c7aca450) is a 64-bit C loader that checks its file path for the substring AOMEI, queries myip.opendns[.]com, checkip.amazonaws[.]com, api.ipify[.]org, and ifconfig[.]me/ip using User-Agents Anyviewer-loader/1.0 and Anyviewer-ipcheck/1.0, and aborts payload execution if the returned country code is CN. It acquires mutex Global\{F9E6E3C0-E11A-4F85-9944-AF4AD6E05883}, downloads component[.]zip (also seen as en[.]zip) from promotion.storage-data[.]com to %TEMP%\svc<random_hex>.tmp, and registers a scheduled task named RadminComponentRuntime (description: "Radmin Component runtime checkable.") to execute %LOCALAPPDATA%\Radmin\FamItrfc.exe --runtimechk every three hours. PE timestamps were stomped to show fabricated 2024 build dates. Staging infrastructure shifted from serv.oss-cn-hongkong.aliyuncs[.]com (April-May) to storage-data[.]com domains (July 1-7), then to storage.googleapis[.]com/aomeiupdate/upgrade-now.zip on July 20 specifically to bypass NRD-blocking proxy filters.
- SHINYROAD runs entirely from %LOCALAPPDATA%\Radmin\ with no native persistence, relying on the CROSSROAD-registered scheduled task. Execution starts when the legitimate signed binary FamItrfc.exe loads the attacker's BlkScrDl.dll via DLL search-order hijacking. BlkScrDl.dll maps config[.]zip into shared memory section Local\963d3c60-d406-4ad6-aa1e-dc8e45061ccf, registers csvc\RuntimeComponent.dll as an in-process COM server under CLSID {21191641-0D7F-4CD9-9572-01AAE6E7851B}, and decrypts metadata.dat with ChaCha20/HMAC-SHA256. The decrypted payload is compiled Python bytecode executed inside an embedded PocketPy interpreter, beaconing to 8.218.65[.]184:443 (earlier variants used raw TCP on port 41397). Late-stage follow-on deployed ADAPTAGENT (Adaptix C2) sideloaded as Eztwain4.dll by NitroPromotion.exe, persisted via scheduled task \NitroRuntime, beaconing to 8.210.84[.]56:6800 every two minutes.
- Server-side remediation by AOMEI does not clean compromised endpoints. Any system that polled for updates during one of the three confirmed tampering windows may still have RadminComponentRuntime and NitroRuntime scheduled tasks running. Hunt now: check for those two task names, inspect %LOCALAPPDATA%\Radmin\ and %LOCALAPPDATA%\Nitro Pro\ for unsigned DLLs (BlkScrDl.dll, Eztwain4.dll), and review proxy logs for Anyviewer-loader/1.0 User-Agent strings and connections to storage-data[.]com, 8.210.84[.]56, 47.239.60[.]117, and 8.218.65[.]184 across the full April-July 2026 window. Four YARA rules (G_APT_Downloader_CROSSROAD_1, G_APT_Backdoor_SHINYROAD_1, G_APT_Backdoor_SHINYROAD_2, G_APT_Launcher_ADAPTAGENT_1) and a GTI IOC collection are in the report.
Practitioner takeaway: Do not validate a supply chain alert by rechecking the vendor's live download URL; by design, UNC7017's files are gone within minutes. Preserve the endpoint-cached Tmphtml\ directory contents immediately, pull proxy and firewall logs timestamped to the exact second the EDR alert fired, and run the provided YARA rules against any host running AOMEI Backupper or AnyViewer that was online during April-July 2026. The scheduled task names RadminComponentRuntime and NitroRuntime are your fastest pivot for scope.

item.title: Help TDS Linked to Hotejka as 20,000+ Cloudflare Pages Domains Host Tech Support Scams
item.description:
Help TDS, a Traffic Distribution System active since 2017, is now linked to Russian-language affiliate program Hotejka and suspected ROI777 rebrand, with over 20,000 Cloudflare Pages domains hosting tech support scams since April 2026.
Key findings:
- Help TDS operates as routing infrastructure for a criminal affiliate program, using PHP code templates injected into compromised WordPress sites via a malicious plugin named "woocommerce_inputs" or custom HTML blocks. The plugin steals WordPress credentials and fetches redirect URLs from C2 servers, with roi777[.]com confirmed as a historical C2 domain used between 2018 and 2020. The TDS is assessed to run on Keitaro, an advertising tracking platform frequently abused by threat actors.
- The redirect chain uses browser fingerprinting, geolocation, IP reputation checks, and headless browser detection to triage victims. Qualifying targets land on fake Microsoft Windows security alert pages using full-screen lock techniques and exit prevention. Victims are instructed to call a fake support number, then socially engineered into installing remote desktop tools like Ultraviewer, handing full machine access to the threat actor. A Hotejka Telegram post from July 17, 2026 references a call center in Germany 🇩🇪 handling 50-100 calls per day.
- Since April 2026, scam landing pages have migrated almost entirely to free Cloudflare Pages infrastructure under the *.pages[.]dev wildcard, with roughly 300 disposable domains created daily and over 20,000 detected to date. This disposable-domain rotation is a deliberate blocklist evasion technique and complicates static IOC-based defenses significantly.
- Help TDS has confirmed traffic handoffs to VexTrio Viper, a large cybercrime affiliate network, and receives inbound victim traffic from approximately 20 affiliate operators including Balada Injector, Detour Dog, and DollyWay, all of which heavily target WordPress sites. Infoblox estimates Hotejka has earned at least several million USD across eight years of operation based on DNS volume analysis and affiliate payout benchmarks.
- The Hotejka/ROI777 lineage traces back to Operation Prowli (exposed June 2018), which deployed r2r2 malware on compromised servers for cryptocurrency mining alongside WordPress traffic monetization fraud. A data leak from ROI777 servers in March 2018 exposed Telegram identities and campaign details, likely prompting the rebrand to Disposable TDS and eventually Help TDS.
Practitioner takeaway: on compromised WordPress investigations, hunt for the "woocommerce_inputs" plugin in wp-content/plugins and audit the wp_options table and active plugin list for unauthorized entries. Outbound DNS queries to *.pages[.]dev at high volume or velocity from a single host are a meaningful signal worth flagging in DNS logs, particularly where the referrer chain passes through known affiliate URL patterns. IOCs, DNS data, and affiliate tracking detail are in the Infoblox report.

item.title: CVE-2026-102764: Critical BeyondTrust Remote Support Zero-Day Exploited by China-Linked Hackers
item.description:
CVE-2026-102764: Critical BeyondTrust Remote Support zero-day, CVSS 4.0 score 9.3, actively exploited in the wild by Chinese 🇨🇳 espionage actor ARMORY CASTLE since at least August 29, 2026.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-102764 is an improper origin validation flaw (CWE-290) in BeyondTrust Remote Support's internal messaging component, affecting versions up to and including 26.2.3. No authentication, no user interaction, and no privileges are required. Exploitation allows arbitrary file operations on the appliance, and in observed intrusions it served as the entry point for full root-level compromise of a device that brokers privileged access across an organization's internal estate.
- Post-exploitation by ARMORY CASTLE (formerly UNC5221, also associated with the name WARP PANDA) followed a structured chain documented by Mandiant. Attackers sent POST requests to an unusual PHP resource, then dropped the SAWFLY webshell as mangoapi.php (SHA-256: dc14e215269a93fdbc4c1a80b984c23faf7af0911c6dbb85309796a6f2ae95fb) in a web-accessible directory. SAWFLY uses a custom Base32 plus RC4 communication layer and only responds to requests containing a specific parameter, returning HTTP 404 to everything else. Privilege escalation followed by copying /bin/sh to /usr/bin/dbus-authd, setting root ownership and the SUID bit. Persistence survived reboots via a startup script named zz-root-persist placed under /home/bomgar/sbin/post_boot.d and modification of /ns/config/sudoers.template to grant the compromised service account passwordless root.
- BARECLAW (SHA-256: 1f19b9a27d79c11bda00a1e8faf74a7fdd683d38ccef1b60df2fd0307e3aa462, binary name ingredi_ws) is a C-based SOCKS5-over-WebSocket tunneler deployed to enable covert lateral movement. The attackers reconfigured /ns/config/haproxy.conf to redirect external HTTPS traffic matching the WebSocket path /uidchanarge to BARECLAW listening on localhost, hiding it from external port scans behind the appliance's legitimate TLS surface. The group also abused the native /ns/sbin/bt-secrets utility to attempt credential and API key extraction from the appliance's secrets vault.
- ARMORY CASTLE conducted systematic anti-forensics: authentication logs, web server records, application logs, PHP logs, and credential-vault access records were deleted from the host. This makes appliance-resident evidence unreliable. The staging path app_84304470%2Ephp was also observed. Attribution is assessed at moderate-to-high confidence, consistent with the group's prior exploitation of edge appliances including Citrix NetScaler and Ivanti Connect Secure.
- Patch status: the BT26-05 patch was shipped to customers October 8, 2026. SaaS instances were fully updated by October 9. Self-hosted customers on versions 24.3.1 through 26.2.3 must apply BT26-05-RS via the appliance management interface now. Appliances older than 24.3.1 require an upgrade before patching. BeyondTrust also released a precautionary patch for Privileged Remote Access, which shares affected code, though no confirmed PRA exploitation has been identified. No public PoC exists as of disclosure.
Practitioner takeaway: any internet-accessible Remote Support appliance in the exploitation window (on or after August 29, 2026) should be treated as potentially compromised regardless of patch status. Before rebooting or rebuilding, preserve memory where possible, snapshot virtual appliances, export the disk, and retain all external firewall, WAF, reverse-proxy, and SIEM records covering the full exposure window. Hunt for mangoapi.php in web-accessible directories, /usr/bin/dbus-authd with the SUID bit set, zz-root-persist in /home/bomgar/sbin/post_boot.d, unexpected modifications to /ns/config/haproxy.conf and /ns/config/sudoers.template, and WebSocket connections to /uidchanarge. Review BeyondTrust audit logs for new API accounts, permission escalations on Jump Items or Teams, and changes to outbound log destinations. Because local logs were wiped in observed intrusions, reconstruction depends entirely on centralized telemetry. Rotate all priority credentials (appliance admins, API client secrets, SAML keys, vault credentials, directory-service bind accounts) only after the appliance is patched, isolated, or rebuilt. IOCs are in the report.

item.title: Analysis of the Infrastructure of ARTEX, a Chinese AI Penetration Testing Tool #4: The Birth of Copy Cat
item.description:
Chinese 🇨🇳 AI-assisted penetration testing framework ARTEX has fragmented into multiple rebranded forks after its GitHub repo went dark, with at least one operator deploying it alongside a live CVE-2026-75650 Magento RCE exploit and an IRC-based PHP implant.
Key findings:
- ARTEX has spawned at least six confirmed rebrands: ScopeWeaver, Tangora PTaaS, Horda, Meze, AegisLoop, and Bob Research Labs / THE GRIM REAPER. The core multi-agent orchestration architecture, PostgreSQL-backed task state, and Planner-plus-three-Workers model carry across all of them, making the shared lineage traceable even when product names and UIs are replaced. Hunt for the reaper-full project name and artex-linux-amd64 references in exposed internal paths.
- The Bob Research Labs / REAPER instance exposed two frontends on TCP ports 3001 and 443, ran LLM profiles backed by DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, and Claude, and carried a bobresearch agent profile. The multi-LLM backend design means operators can swap inference providers without restructuring the attack pipeline, a capability gap that commodity red-team tooling does not yet reflect.
- CVE-2026-75650, an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw in Magento/Adobe Commerce, was actively staged in the Bob Research Labs environment using StyleSmuggler, the public PoC. Evidence of execution steps was present: Guest Cart creation, billing information manipulation, triggering the vulnerable checkout flow, and extraction of the Magento Report Identifier. The follow-up dropped cache.php and testnewbot.php, and an "IRC BOT DEPLOYED" message was logged.
- irc.php functions as a persistence-anchored IRC C2 implant. It connects to the password-protected channel mg_master, installs itself via an [@]reboot cron job, copies itself to hidden paths, supports multiple PHP execution functions, and accepts !Cmd@ and !Cmd@all commands for remote tasking. This is post-exploitation infrastructure, not a scanner artifact.
- Korean localization artifacts are widespread across forks: Korean strings embedded in Go code handling SMTP, Notes, and HTTP processing; a translate_go.py script mapping Korean and Chinese 🇨🇳 strings to English; and an artex-ko directory. Skills packages (skills-en-keep, skills-backup, skills-translated-en[.]zip, bob-research-skills-en[.]zip) show a deliberate workflow of collecting, translating, and repackaging attack playbooks covering SQL injection, SSRF, XSS, XXE, IDOR, command injection, cloud and container testing, and more.
Practitioner takeaway: If you work Magento incident response, look for cache.php, testnewbot.php, and irc.php in the webroot and cache directories. Check crontabs for [@]reboot entries pointing to PHP processes and outbound IRC connections from the web tier. item.content:encoded:
Chinese 🇨🇳 AI-assisted penetration testing framework ARTEX has fragmented into multiple rebranded forks after its GitHub repo went dark, with at least one operator deploying it alongside a live CVE-2026-75650 Magento RCE exploit and an IRC-based PHP implant.

Key findings:

- ARTEX has spawned at least six confirmed rebrands: ScopeWeaver, Tangora PTaaS, Horda, Meze, AegisLoop, and Bob Research Labs / THE GRIM REAPER. The core multi-agent orchestration architecture, PostgreSQL-backed task state, and Planner-plus-three-Workers model carry across all of them, making the shared lineage traceable even when product names and UIs are replaced. Hunt for the reaper-full project name and artex-linux-amd64 references in exposed internal paths.

- The Bob Research Labs / REAPER instance exposed two frontends on TCP ports 3001 and 443, ran LLM profiles backed by DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, and Claude, and carried a bobresearch agent profile. The multi-LLM backend design means operators can swap inference providers without restructuring the attack pipeline, a capability gap that commodity red-team tooling does not yet reflect.

- CVE-2026-75650, an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw in Magento/Adobe Commerce, was actively staged in the Bob Research Labs environment using StyleSmuggler, the public PoC. Evidence of execution steps was present: Guest Cart creation, billing information manipulation, triggering the vulnerable checkout flow, and extraction of the Magento Report Identifier. The follow-up dropped cache.php and testnewbot.php, and an "IRC BOT DEPLOYED" message was logged.

- irc.php functions as a persistence-anchored IRC C2 implant. It connects to the password-protected channel mg_master, installs itself via an [@]reboot cron job, copies itself to hidden paths, supports multiple PHP execution functions, and accepts !Cmd@ and !Cmd@all commands for remote tasking. This is post-exploitation infrastructure, not a scanner artifact.

- Korean localization artifacts are widespread across forks: Korean strings embedded in Go code handling SMTP, Notes, and HTTP processing; a translate_go.py script mapping Korean and Chinese 🇨🇳 strings to English; and an artex-ko directory. Skills packages (skills-en-keep, skills-backup, skills-translated-en[.]zip, bob-research-skills-en[.]zip) show a deliberate workflow of collecting, translating, and repackaging attack playbooks covering SQL injection, SSRF, XSS, XXE, IDOR, command injection, cloud and container testing, and more.

Practitioner takeaway: If you work Magento incident response, look for cache.php, testnewbot.php, and irc.php in the webroot and cache directories. Check crontabs for [@]reboot entries pointing to PHP processes and outbound IRC connections from the web tier. For threat hunters tracking ARTEX-lineage infrastructure, exposed PostgreSQL instances with task-state tables, dual-port frontends (3001/443), and artex-linux-amd64 binary references in process or path artifacts are the fingerprint. The AhnLab ASEC report documents IOCs, credential exposures, and runtime artifacts found in the wild.

item.title: China Espionage Actor Actively Targeting Critical BeyondTrust Flaw, Google Warns
item.description:
Chinese 🇨🇳 espionage actor Armory Castle exploited critical BeyondTrust flaw CVE-2026-102764 (CVSS 9.3) in August 2026, achieving root-level persistence on Remote Support appliances before public disclosure.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-102764 (CVSS 9.3) in BeyondTrust Remote Support was exploited by Armory Castle as a zero-day in August 2026. BeyondTrust disclosed it October 15, 2026, with patches available for SaaS and self-hosted customers since October 8. Google warns broad opportunistic exploitation is now likely given public disclosure.
- Post-exploitation centered on a PHP webshell named Sawfly, deployed with bidirectional encrypted C2. Armory Castle then copied the system shell to /usr/bin/dbus-authd, set SUID permissions and root ownership, creating a persistent root backdoor that survives reboots and configuration resets. They also modified BeyondTrust configuration templates to grant passwordless root to the site service account.
- Credential harvesting targeted the appliance's native secrets database using /ns/sbin/bt-secrets, a proprietary BeyondTrust CLI utility for managing passwords, API keys, and endpoint credentials. Directly brokered credentials stored on the appliance were at risk. The actor also elevated a compromised account's Jump Item and Team permissions from No Access to Administrator, granting unrestricted ability to launch remote sessions to downstream systems.
- Lateral movement used a tunneler named Bareclaw to route traffic through the compromised BeyondTrust device. Sensitive internal documents, including software inventories, were exfiltrated via BeyondTrust's native file transfer service directly from user desktops. Armory Castle then systematically deleted system, web server, and application logs to hinder detection.
- Armory Castle has been active since October 2023, conducting long-term intelligence collection for the People's Republic of China 🇨🇳, targeting legal services, SaaS providers, business-process outsourcers, technology companies, and government entities. Google assesses with high confidence this actor will continue leveraging zero-day flaws in edge devices for espionage.
Responder priority: preserve all available telemetry before taking containment action, Google explicitly flags this. Hunt for /usr/bin/dbus-authd as an anomalous SUID binary, any PHP webshells on the appliance, and unexpected use of /ns/sbin/bt-secrets. Check Jump Item and Team permission changes in the appliance audit log. Any appliance with confirmed or unknown compromise status should be rebuilt from a clean, fully patched image, not just patched in place. Rotate all credentials the appliance stored or brokered, in dependency order, after isolation.

item.title: PEERSTITCH malware: How Attackers Compromised 500 Firewalls Through FortiManager
item.description:
CL-STA-0954 hit a telecom MSP's FortiManager with CVE-2024-47575, exfiltrating credentials and configs for 500+ downstream firewalls, then deployed the memory-only PEERSTITCH implant via a second CVE to maintain covert access.
Key findings:
- Initial access exploited CVE-2024-47575 (FortiJump), an unauthenticated flaw allowing a rogue virtual device to register with FortiManager over TCP port 541. Within minutes, the attackers extracted a configuration archive containing serial numbers, public IPs, routing tables, VPN credentials, and cryptographic trust material for every managed FortiGate. Passwords were stored as reversible ciphertext, so decryption was trivial. Those stolen keys remain valid until individually rotated on every managed device. Patching FortiManager does not invalidate them.
- A second vulnerability, CVE-2025-61624, a path traversal flaw in the FortiOS auto-script engine, was used to deploy PEERSTITCH. Before execution, the attackers killed the logging and syslog daemons to suppress evidence, wiped crash logs, auto-deleted rogue admin accounts and script objects post-execution, overwrote the malicious ACME config file with benign text, and unlinked the injector binary from disk.
- PEERSTITCH is a 64-bit ARM64 binary written in C that leaves no persistent file on disk, opens no listening ports, and makes no outbound connections. It injects into two legitimate FortiOS daemons, the logging process and the VPN service, using already-allocated memory. It watches for traffic carrying two specific markers (an embedded port number and a link-local IP) in the logging daemon, extracts a session token, and writes it directly into VPN daemon memory via Linux's /proc filesystem, creating a covert bridge between legitimate processes. Fortinet's Integrity Checker Tool cannot detect it because it only scans files on disk, which remain untouched.
- A secondary command channel abused Apache's built-in certificate management module: shell commands were embedded in the domain name field of certificate validation requests, with Apache configured to retry them continuously, creating a persistent outbound reverse shell through a legitimate system process. The attackers also impersonated the FortiManager platform to pull from managed firewalls of other hosts in the targeted network.
- Scope matters here. This was an MSP. The 500+ firewalls included both the provider's own infrastructure and its clients' networks. Those downstream organizations had no visibility into what was happening. Unit 42's investigation covered only the provider's environment, not the affected clients. A single management platform breach became a supply-chain incident.
Practitioner takeaway: Fortinet's Integrity Checker Tool will not find PEERSTITCH. Detection requires live memory inspection of the FortiOS logging and VPN daemons, specifically looking for anomalous read-write-execute (RWX) memory regions or NOP patches at unexpected offsets in daemon code. For any FortiManager compromise involving CVE-2024-47575, treat all cryptographic trust material and VPN credentials as fully compromised regardless of patch status, and begin rotation across every managed device. Isolate management interfaces at the network level and audit for unauthorized SSL/VPN sessions originating from external addresses into internal management segments.

item.title: Silent Lynx Exploits WinRAR Flaw to Deploy Reverse Shell in CIS Government Attacks
item.description:
Kazakhstan-nexus Silent Lynx (UAT-6275 / TAG-193) hits CIS government targets across nine countries over 14 months, escalating from macro-laced docs to active CVE exploitation in its latest infection chain.
Key details:
- Silent Lynx ran at least eight phishing campaigns between January 2025 and May 2026, targeting Kazakhstan 🇰🇿, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Russia 🇷🇺, and Belarus 🇧🇾. Spearphishing emails originate from compromised government accounts and carry lures themed around diplomacy, international trade, energy, and aviation, including a diplomatic letter to Armenia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, a Turkmenistan airspace application form, and a business proposal tied to Russia's 🇷🇺 Orsk Oil Refinery. That level of lure specificity points to prior access and open-source research on targets.
- Four distinct infection chains were observed across the campaign window. June 2025 used macro-enabled Word documents to pull and execute a second-stage binary. July 2025 used PS2EXE-packaged PowerShell executables as downloaders, with scheduled tasks created for persistence. October 2025 introduced a malicious LNK inside a RAR archive, launching PowerShell to retrieve a GitHub-hosted script providing remote shell access, with subsequent iterations also dropping PickleShell into the Windows Startup folder for login-triggered persistence. April 2026 weaponized CVE-2025-8088, a WinRAR flaw, to extract PickleShell directly into the Windows Startup folder, the group's first documented use of a CVE as a delivery mechanism.
- The custom reverse shells deployed across campaigns include FoalShell, Chvost, Laplas, and PickleShell. Each provides interactive remote access to compromised hosts. PickleShell in particular appears across multiple infection chains and is staged in the Windows Startup folder, making it a key persistence artifact to hunt. The group's tooling overlaps with clusters tracked as YoroTrooper, ShadowSilk, Cavalry Werewolf, and Tomiris, though Cisco Talos notes no direct indicator or toolset overlap has been confirmed between UAT-6275 and YoroTrooper specifically.
- Three publicly accessible staging directories linked to the actor were found hosting Linux-compatible tooling and a public proof-of-concept exploit for CVE-2025-25257, an SQL injection vulnerability in Fortinet FortiWeb. This signals a likely capability expansion beyond Windows endpoints toward internet-facing web application infrastructure, a meaningful shift for a group previously focused on endpoint-level access via phishing.
- Targeting priorities center on environmental agencies, economic ministries, and energy infrastructure across Central Asia and the broader CIS region. Related cluster Hydra Saiga (also tracked as Comrade Saiga) compromised at least 34 organizations across 8 countries since December 2024 with custom implants written in Rust, Go, and Python alongside living-off-the-land techniques, with reconnaissance extending to over 200 additional targets globally.
DFIR focus: Hunt the Windows Startup folder for PickleShell presence, especially on systems running WinRAR where CVE-2025-8088 may have been triggered by opening a crafted archive. Review scheduled tasks created around July 2025 campaign timeframes for PS2EXE-built executables. For October 2025-era intrusions, examine LNK execution followed by PowerShell reaching out to GitHub for hosted scripts. On network-facing Fortinet FortiWeb instances, assess exposure to CVE-2025-25257 and review web logs for SQL injection patterns. The Cisco Talos and Recorded Future Insikt Group reports are the primary sources for IOCs and campaign detail.

item.title: [0day-rubbish] Maian Guardian 2.1 license generator projid command injection to www-data uid 33 code execution (7.2, PR:H)
item.description:
Maian Guardian 2.1 carries an OS command injection in its license generator that gives an authenticated administrator arbitrary code execution as www-data. No CVE assigned yet; CVSS 3.1 base score 7.2 High (PR:H).
Key findings:
- The root cause is a dead sanitizer arrangement in control/classes/class.licensing.php. The escape() function at lines 68-70 returns its input unchanged, mswCD() at lines 152-154 is a second return $data stub stacked in front of it, and escapeArg() which correctly calls escapeshellarg() has no call site anywhere across the 308 PHP files in the shipped tree. The result: projid, projkey, property key/value pairs, and the encoder string all arrive from a POST to /admin/index.php?ajax-ops=generate, pass through two no-ops, and land inside double-quoted words in a shell_exec() call. A projid of $(id) executes in a subshell during argument expansion, before the command word resolves, so the injection fires even when the SourceGuardian generator binary is absent or misconfigured.
- The CVSS vector is CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H = 7.2. PR:H carries the weight: exploitation requires an authenticated administrator session. Eight authentication bypass paths were examined and all eight were blocked. Unauthenticated RCE was not reached and is not claimed.
- Impact as demonstrated: six distinct OS commands executed as uid=33(www-data) in a single authenticated POST, including a pipeline. A file written into the document root was served back over HTTP, which in a PHP-executing web tree is a durable implant reachable by unauthenticated visitors after the fact. The advisory argues (not demonstrated in the recorded run) that the same identity can read control/_cfg.php to recover database credentials, SECRET_KEY, and the API key. SECRET_KEY concatenated with a timestamp produces a valid guardian_access session value, meaning an attacker who reads it can forge administrator sessions with no login event logged.
- Detection is constrained by design. The triggering request logs as a plain POST /admin/index.php?ajax-ops=generate with HTTP 200 and no error status, because the request body is not logged and the application returned its normal {"status":"rdr"} response. The advisory recommends alerting on any generate request body containing $( or its percent-encoded form %24%28 at the proxy layer, watching for /bin/sh -c child processes descended from the web server with argument lists containing redirections or semicolons, file-integrity monitoring on the document tree for new service-account-owned files, and auditing guardian_access sessions against login events as a high-signal post-compromise indicator.
Practitioner takeaway: until a patch ships, treat Maian Guardian administrator credentials as equivalent to shell access on the licensing host. The advisory's mitigation priority is replacing shell_exec() at class.licensing.php:261 with a proc_open() array invocation so no shell is spawned at all. If you are scoping an incident, check the document root for unexpected files owned by www-data, cross-reference active guardian_access sessions against the access log for a corresponding login request, and rotate SECRET_KEY, the API key, the administrator credential, and database credentials if compromise is suspected. No CVE ID has been assigned; no patch exists at time of disclosure.

item.title: PEERSTITCH Malware Deployed via FortiOS Flaw Bypasses Checks on Tagged VPN Sessions
item.description:
Suspected APT deploys PEERSTITCH, a memory-resident ARM64 implant, via FortiOS path traversal flaw CVE-2025-61624, achieving persistent VPN session hijacking with no disk artifacts, no listening ports, and no outbound connections.
Key findings:
- CVE-2025-61624 (CVSS 5.4) is a path traversal flaw in the FortiOS command line interpreter, also affecting FortiPAM, FortiProxy, and FortiSwitchManager. It was patched by Fortinet in April 2026. Initial access to this intrusion chain (tracked as CL-STA-0954 / UNC5820) began earlier via FortiJump (CVE-2024-47575), a critical FortiManager flaw. That first foothold enabled exfiltration of running configs, private keys, SSL/VPN credentials, and an inventory of more than 500 managed FortiGate serial numbers with public IPs. The stolen trust material powered every subsequent stage.
- PEERSTITCH arrives as a 64-bit Linux ARM64 ELF binary and is staged by an auto-script that pulls five components from 23.240.77[.]233:8085: an environment prep script (pM.js, self-deleting), an Emscripten JS runtime (a.js saved as index.js), a WebAssembly module (a.wasm saved as index.wasm), an orchestrator (b.js saved as ipssem.js), and the core injector ELF (dd saved as lldprx). After an execution delay, ipssem.js launches lldprx, which uses ptrace (PTRACE_INTERRUPT) to attach to the live FortiOS daemons /bin/miglogd and /bin/iked, allocates executable memory inside each process, writes malicious hooks, and redirects execution without touching disk again.
- The hooks create a covert inter-process communication bridge between miglogd and iked entirely inside process memory. The miglogd hook watches passing traffic for two markers: TCP port 8550 embedded in traffic data and link-local IP 169.254.0.1 as a pattern-match identifier. When both match, a session token is handed to the iked hook, which then recognizes that token in subsequent VPN session buffers and routes those sessions down an alternative code path, bypassing FortiOS security validations. The result is persistent, undetected VPN session hijacking with no listening socket and no new network connection from the implant itself.
- CL-STA-0954 also abused the native Apache mod_md module on FortiGate devices to spawn an SSH-based reverse shell as a separate C2 channel, and impersonated the FortiManager platform to pivot into managed firewalls across client networks. The actors actively suppressed forensics by terminating syslog generation, clearing crash logs, disrupting logging telemetry, and auto-deleting rogue administrator accounts and auto-script objects after execution.
- The scope of pre-positioned access is significant: configs, routing tables, internal topology maps, and private keys for more than 500 downstream FortiGate firewalls were harvested from a single FortiManager compromise. Unit 42 notes the actors demonstrated deep familiarity with FortiOS internals and management protocols.

item.content:encoded:
Suspected APT deploys PEERSTITCH, a memory-resident ARM64 implant, via FortiOS path traversal flaw CVE-2025-61624, achieving persistent VPN session hijacking with no disk artifacts, no listening ports, and no outbound connections.

Key findings:

- CVE-2025-61624 (CVSS 5.4) is a path traversal flaw in the FortiOS command line interpreter, also affecting FortiPAM, FortiProxy, and FortiSwitchManager. It was patched by Fortinet in April 2026. Initial access to this intrusion chain (tracked as CL-STA-0954 / UNC5820) began earlier via FortiJump (CVE-2024-47575), a critical FortiManager flaw. That first foothold enabled exfiltration of running configs, private keys, SSL/VPN credentials, and an inventory of more than 500 managed FortiGate serial numbers with public IPs. The stolen trust material powered every subsequent stage.

- PEERSTITCH arrives as a 64-bit Linux ARM64 ELF binary and is staged by an auto-script that pulls five components from 23.240.77[.]233:8085: an environment prep script (pM.js, self-deleting), an Emscripten JS runtime (a.js saved as index.js), a WebAssembly module (a.wasm saved as index.wasm), an orchestrator (b.js saved as ipssem.js), and the core injector ELF (dd saved as lldprx). After an execution delay, ipssem.js launches lldprx, which uses ptrace (PTRACE_INTERRUPT) to attach to the live FortiOS daemons /bin/miglogd and /bin/iked, allocates executable memory inside each process, writes malicious hooks, and redirects execution without touching disk again.

- The hooks create a covert inter-process communication bridge between miglogd and iked entirely inside process memory. The miglogd hook watches passing traffic for two markers: TCP port 8550 embedded in traffic data and link-local IP 169.254.0.1 as a pattern-match identifier. When both match, a session token is handed to the iked hook, which then recognizes that token in subsequent VPN session buffers and routes those sessions down an alternative code path, bypassing FortiOS security validations. The result is persistent, undetected VPN session hijacking with no listening socket and no new network connection from the implant itself.

- CL-STA-0954 also abused the native Apache mod_md module on FortiGate devices to spawn an SSH-based reverse shell as a separate C2 channel, and impersonated the FortiManager platform to pivot into managed firewalls across client networks. The actors actively suppressed forensics by terminating syslog generation, clearing crash logs, disrupting logging telemetry, and auto-deleting rogue administrator accounts and auto-script objects after execution.

- The scope of pre-positioned access is significant: configs, routing tables, internal topology maps, and private keys for more than 500 downstream FortiGate firewalls were harvested from a single FortiManager compromise. Unit 42 notes the actors demonstrated deep familiarity with FortiOS internals and management protocols.

DFIR takeaway: conventional disk and network IOC hunts will miss PEERSTITCH entirely. Focus on process memory and runtime behavior. Look for ptrace calls against miglogd and iked from unexpected parent processes, unexpected executable memory regions in those daemon processes, and any process spawned by Apache mod_md that initiates SSH outbound. Audit FortiManager enrollment logs and admin account creation events for accounts deleted after short lifespans. Check for the C2 staging IP 23.240.77[.]233 in firewall and proxy logs across the September 2024 to April 2026 window. The Unit 42 report contains IOCs for this campaign.

item.title: (TLP:CLEAR) Joint Advisory Exposes China-Linked Integrity Tech’s Tools and Tactics for Stealing Sensitive Data
item.description:
Chinese 🇨🇳 state-linked company Integrity Technology Group exposed as enabler of Flax Typhoon, Ethereal Panda, and Red Juliett operations targeting US 🇺🇸 critical infrastructure, with FBI seizing seven operational domains in a coordinated takedown.
Key details:
- Integrity Tech, a Chinese 🇨🇳 government-linked company, provides tooling and infrastructure to actors tracked under multiple aliases including Flax Typhoon, Ethereal Panda, and Red Juliett. Targeted sectors include US 🇺🇸 government, critical manufacturing, healthcare, and IT. The tradecraft combines automated scanning via a proprietary tool called MicroScan with hands-on exploitation of known CVEs, some going back to 2014, meaning unpatched legacy appliances are explicitly in scope.
- The attack chain moves from automated internet-facing reconnaissance through credential theft, using cross-site scripting and password spraying against Microsoft Exchange, into persistent access established by deploying the legitimate SoftEther VPN client disguised as native Windows processes. SoftEther is a real, signed tool, which means it rarely trips signature-based alerts. The advisory names conhost.exe and dllhost.exe running outside System32 as the masquerade pattern to hunt.
- Persistence and lateral movement can bridge IT and OT environments where network segmentation is weak. Credentials stolen from webmail or remote access systems can become the entry point into operational technology networks, a specific concern for utilities running aging VPN appliances, FTP servers, or self-hosted web applications that match the broad scanning profile these actors use.
- The FBI seized seven domains tied to MicroScan and FishHub, a spear-phishing tool used in the same campaign. Some IOCs in the advisory date back to 2016, so retrospective log searches are warranted, but vet aged indicators against your environment before blocking to avoid false positives.
Practitioner takeaway: Hunt for SoftEther VPN client binaries running outside expected paths, and flag conhost.exe or dllhost.exe processes whose image path is not System32. Monitor for unexpected Active Directory replication requests originating from hosts that are not domain controllers, a common indicator of credential harvesting at scale. The joint advisory's Appendix B lists the exploited CVEs for patch and exposure checks, and the IOC set is available in the advisory for ingestion into detection tooling and historical log review.

item.title: Citizen Lab Traces Zero-Click Candiru Spyware Infections at Al Jazeera to Targeted Online Ads
item.description:
Zero-click mercenary spyware delivered via programmatic advertising confirmed in live attacks against Al Jazeera, marking the first public technical proof that government-grade hacking tools reached real devices through ordinary online ads.
Key findings:
- The attack chain required no user interaction. When a Discover-Tech ad loaded, embedded code silently exfiltrated the device's advertising ID and IP address to a Discover-Tech server. That server screened the device against a target list and, if matched, returned browser or app exploit code on the fly. Unmatched devices received nothing, meaning the ad networks carrying the ads had no malicious payload to scan. At least 45 devices at Al Jazeera were targeted across 2024 and 2025. The connection sequence logged in Al Jazeera's traffic: Discover-Tech ad server, then a Candiru screening server, then a C2 server running the spyware.
- The recovered Windows executable ties this operation to Candiru with high confidence. The SHA-256 of the spyware sample is 255869de85e2a171993fc5eb8a556d873a1b8966e040f6f55926f2fa2d595cc8. Its code shared distinctive techniques with a Candiru implant Citizen Lab dissected in 2021. The exploit stage itself was not recovered from any device, so the browser or app vulnerability used to install the payload remains unidentified from captured code alone. The attributing government customer was not named.
- Discover-Tech's infrastructure reached far beyond the target. Between March and June 2026 the company placed nearly four billion ad bids on one platform alone, with the callback-carrying ads appearing across roughly 75,000 phone apps and 120,000 websites. Confiant estimated roughly 10 million ads per day. Affected networks included NATO, UN bodies, EU institutions, government offices in approximately two dozen countries, chipmakers, and news organizations. Ad reach is not proof of infection: it demonstrates the targeting surface available to the operator.
- The campaign stayed hidden inside legitimate ad infrastructure for years. Discover-Tech, registered in Israel 🇮🇱 in 2020, held approved vendor status with both Google and IAB Europe until early October 2026. Candiru itself was placed on a US 🇺🇸 trade blacklist in 2021, then its assets were acquired by Integrity Partners and reportedly restructured into Integrity Labs, a move the report says sits outside the existing sanctions. The primary ad server domain tied to the operation is mtrtb[.]com.
DFIR takeaway: If your organization appears on the list of networks where Discover-Tech ads were observed, treat any device on that network during the exposure window as potentially targeted. Hunt your DNS, proxy, and network flow logs for the three-hop sequence: a request to mtrtb[.]com, followed by connections to Candiru screening infrastructure, followed by C2 activity. The spyware hash (255869de85e2a171993fc5eb8a556d873a1b8966e040f6f55926f2fa2d595cc8) is your primary file-based indicator on Windows endpoints. The full command-and-control domain list, additional indicators, and associated files are published in Confiant's report alongside the Citizen Lab findings: pull those before building your blocklist and running retrospective log searches.

item.title: VestaCP <= 0.9.8-26: authenticated config-parser eval sinks -> root RCE (VESTACP-2026-001)
item.description:
VESTACP-2026-001: Abandoned VestaCP panel carries a CVSS 9.9 authenticated eval-injection chain that hands an ordinary hosting tenant full root on the entire host node, with no upstream fix possible.
Key findings:
- The vulnerability lives in func/main.sh, the shared shell library sourced by every v-* administration script in VestaCP. Those scripts run as root. The library parses per-account config files (domains, cron jobs, DNS, mail, users stored as KEY='value' lines under USER_DATA/*.conf) using eval, so a crafted value containing an unescaped single quote breaks out of the quoted assignment and executes arbitrary shell as root. Affected sinks named in the advisory include is_object_value_empty, is_object_value_exist, get_object_value, update_object_value, add_object_key, search_objects, sync_cron_jobs, the ARGUMENTS builder, is_format_valid, and the unquoted echo $7 in v-add-cron-job (the crontab injection subclass). This is VESTACP-2026-001, CVSS:3.1 9.9, CWE-78 and CWE-95.
- Exploitation requires only an authenticated panel account, meaning any shared-hosting tenant qualifies. A malicious cron CMD field such as CMD='x'; id > /tmp/pwned; # is stored in a .conf file, then the injected commands fire the next time any root-owned v-* script parses that object, including during routine panel operations and scheduled sync jobs. No further attacker interaction is needed after the value is written. The result is a tenant-to-host escape: full root access exposing every site, mailbox, and database on the node.
- VestaCP has been abandoned since September 2019 and will never receive a patch. The same eval-sink class was identified and fixed in the downstream HestiaCP fork (GHSA-w3mx-xq85-8qqc, patched in 1.9.5), but VestaCP itself never received the fix. The advisory notes VestaCP remains deployed in production, including in Virtualizor VPS templates still offered by hosting providers, making the exposure broader than a typical end-of-life product.
- The advisory's repository contains a self-contained PoC (poc/poc-eval-sink.sh) simulating the vulnerable parse, a drop-in non-eval replacement parser (mitigation/non-eval-parser.sh) using strict KEY='value' regex and declare -g assignment so values become literals and are never executed, and a porting recipe covering all eval sites in the codebase.
Responder takeaway: if VestaCP appears in your environment, start by auditing USER_DATA/*.conf files across all tenant accounts for values containing unescaped single quotes, semicolons, or shell metacharacters, particularly in CMD fields, domain alias fields, and DNS records. Any such value that predates your investigation is a potential indicator of prior exploitation or staging. Monitor those conf files for unexpected writes as a detection control. The drop-in parser and porting recipe are in the advisory repository at github[.]com/sysdopllc/vestacp-config-eval-rce. There is no vendor path forward: migration to a maintained control panel is the only durable fix.

item.title: Aoki: Infostealer Targets AI Coding Assistant Credentials
item.description:
Aoki infostealer adds AI coding assistant credential theft to its target list, harvesting API keys and session tokens for Claude, Codex, Cursor, Gemini, and more in what appears to be an actively expanding capability added in 2026.
Key findings:
- Aoki (aka Aokigahara), first observed earlier in 2026, has been updated to specifically target .claude.json, Claude desktop cookies, ChatGPT cookies, Codex config.toml and .env files, along with tokens for GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Google Gemini, JetBrains AI Assistant, Kiro, and AWS credentials. Older samples did not target AI-related files, confirming this is a deliberate, recent expansion of scope, not a legacy feature.
- Stolen AI credentials enable what the report describes as LLMjacking: running up usage costs under the victim's API quota, or reselling the keys outright. More critically, OAuth and session tokens can expose connected repositories, cloud services, and CI/CD pipelines, giving an attacker a pivot into a developer's broader environment under a trusted identity. Cursor's local state database is also targeted because it can cache chat context and code snippets.
- Beyond AI tooling, the most current sample sweeps an exceptionally wide surface: cookies, autofill data, and saved passwords from roughly 40 browsers; extensions and desktop wallets for over 80 cryptocurrency targets; Discord tokens from 13 Discord-related clients; Telegram session data from 8 forks; gaming credentials for Steam, Roblox, Epic Games, and others; VPN configs for OpenVPN, NordVPN, ProtonVPN, PIA, Surfshark, and Windscribe; FTP clients; password managers including KeePass, Bitwarden, and 1Password; and Outlook passwords pulled from the registry. It also enumerates installed security products and records them. The malware has no interactive backdoor: it collects everything available and ships it to C2 via a /gate endpoint.
- C2 infrastructure has shifted across generations. Older samples communicated over unencrypted HTTP to an IP address on port 8080. Newer samples use HTTPS to dedicated domains. Active C2 domains from the report: dobeqnesmot[.]cc, hjazfioe[.]surf, and neihite[.]cc, all reached via a /gate path (hxxps://dobeqnesmot[.]cc/gate, hxxps://hjazfioe[.]surf/gate, hxxps://neihite[.]cc/gate). Attribution is unknown: Symantec found no links to existing malware families and has not identified a threat group.
- 18 file hashes are published in the Symantec report alongside the network IOCs above. The decryption routine contains the string "Aokigahara," which is how the family was named. Symantec detects it as Infostealer.Aoki.
Practitioner takeaway: on developer endpoints and CI/CD build agents, hunt for unexpected reads of .claude.json, config.toml, .env files in AI assistant directories, and token files for Cursor and Copilot, especially followed by outbound HTTPS to .cc or .surf domains hitting a /gate path. Check for Outlook credential reads from HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Office and Mozilla Thunderbird profile access, which are reliable stealer artifacts on Windows hosts. The IOCs and file hashes are in the Symantec report and should be ingested into your threat intel pipeline now, particularly given developer machines' access to source code repositories and cloud credentials.

item.title: Inside Help TDS: Hotejka, Cloudflare Pages and Predictive Detection
item.description:
Help TDS, a tech support scam network active since 2017, is now attributed to Hotejka, a rebranded Russian-language affiliate program generating ~300 malicious Cloudflare Pages domains daily and paying affiliates up to $100 per routed call.
- Hotejka is assessed with high confidence to be a rebrand of ROI777, exposed in 2018. Attribution rests on shared infrastructure: the IP 162.244.35[.]33 hosted roi777[.]com until March 2022 and then resolved to hotejka[.]com as its PTR record. Affiliate IDs (u=h2xkd0) tracked across multiple C2 generations tie both entities to the same two European affiliate advertising platforms, which Infoblox estimates have paid the operator several million USD since 2017. Known affiliates feeding traffic into Help TDS include Balada Injector, Detour Dog, and DollyWay.
- The attack chain starts at a compromised website, malvertising, spam, or a Telegram bot (freeassistant_bot). The victim hits a Cloudflare Pages domain that browser-fingerprints and geofilters them, then serves a browser-lock scareware page impersonating Microsoft. The lure PHP code resolves the active C2 by polling the Telegram channel trafficredirect, falls back to a JSON endpoint at pinkfels[.]shop, caches the result in base64, and gates display to U.S. 🇺🇸 working hours computed in Moscow time (16:00-00:59 MSK, Monday through Friday). The victim is funneled to a call center and instructed to download UltraViewer from ultraviewer[.]net, handing the operator full remote access.
- The CNAME affiliate path is a separate, DNS-level redirect: an affiliate domain such as fosetya[.]shop carries a CNAME record pointing to hotcname[.]help (recently resolving to 91.196.33[.]144, AS207957 SERV[.]HOST). Traffic arrives at the affiliate, DNS transparently forwards it to Hotejka's server, and the victim lands on a tech support scam page. This same IP hosts usa.on1xvpn[.]com and usa.on1xvpn[.]ru, a Russian-language VPN service, though the nature of that relationship is not yet confirmed.
- Scale and infrastructure: since April 2026, Hotejka has announced roughly 300 new pages[.]dev subdomains daily via Telegram, rotating domains approximately weekly. Infoblox detected over 30,000 domains in six months, 16,000 of which were later confirmed in the Telegram C2 channel. A predictive detection algorithm, deployed in July 2026, now identifies domains a median of seven days before they appear in that channel, reducing customer exposure from 4% on peak days to under 0.5% in September. September 2026 Telegram posts also announced a forthcoming forced browser extension installation capability.
Practitioner takeaway: hunt for the WordPress plugin and PHP lure code in your environment by looking for base64-encoded cache files and outbound resolution of hotcname[.]help or pinkfels[.]shop. For DNS responders, CNAME chains terminating at hotcname[.]help are a reliable pivot. IOCs including Hotejka domains, IPs (62.113.117[.]248, 91.196.33[.]144), affiliate domains (fosetya[.]shop, zylvantrexor[.]lol, goalods[.]lol, trixsolvesxa[.]shop), Cloudflare Pages samples (arrow-berry-gem.pages[.]dev, linen-thorn-wild.pages[.]dev), Telegram handles, and call center numbers are listed in the report.

item.content:encoded:
Help TDS, a tech support scam network active since 2017, is now attributed to Hotejka, a rebranded Russian-language affiliate program generating ~300 malicious Cloudflare Pages domains daily and paying affiliates up to $100 per routed call.

- Hotejka is assessed with high confidence to be a rebrand of ROI777, exposed in 2018. Attribution rests on shared infrastructure: the IP 162.244.35[.]33 hosted roi777[.]com until March 2022 and then resolved to hotejka[.]com as its PTR record. Affiliate IDs (u=h2xkd0) tracked across multiple C2 generations tie both entities to the same two European affiliate advertising platforms, which Infoblox estimates have paid the operator several million USD since 2017. Known affiliates feeding traffic into Help TDS include Balada Injector, Detour Dog, and DollyWay.

- The attack chain starts at a compromised website, malvertising, spam, or a Telegram bot (freeassistant_bot). The victim hits a Cloudflare Pages domain that browser-fingerprints and geofilters them, then serves a browser-lock scareware page impersonating Microsoft. The lure PHP code resolves the active C2 by polling the Telegram channel trafficredirect, falls back to a JSON endpoint at pinkfels[.]shop, caches the result in base64, and gates display to U.S. 🇺🇸 working hours computed in Moscow time (16:00-00:59 MSK, Monday through Friday). The victim is funneled to a call center and instructed to download UltraViewer from ultraviewer[.]net, handing the operator full remote access.

- The CNAME affiliate path is a separate, DNS-level redirect: an affiliate domain such as fosetya[.]shop carries a CNAME record pointing to hotcname[.]help (recently resolving to 91.196.33[.]144, AS207957 SERV[.]HOST). Traffic arrives at the affiliate, DNS transparently forwards it to Hotejka's server, and the victim lands on a tech support scam page. This same IP hosts usa.on1xvpn[.]com and usa.on1xvpn[.]ru, a Russian-language VPN service, though the nature of that relationship is not yet confirmed.

- Scale and infrastructure: since April 2026, Hotejka has announced roughly 300 new pages[.]dev subdomains daily via Telegram, rotating domains approximately weekly. Infoblox detected over 30,000 domains in six months, 16,000 of which were later confirmed in the Telegram C2 channel. A predictive detection algorithm, deployed in July 2026, now identifies domains a median of seven days before they appear in that channel, reducing customer exposure from 4% on peak days to under 0.5% in September. September 2026 Telegram posts also announced a forthcoming forced browser extension installation capability.

Practitioner takeaway: hunt for the WordPress plugin and PHP lure code in your environment by looking for base64-encoded cache files and outbound resolution of hotcname[.]help or pinkfels[.]shop. For DNS responders, CNAME chains terminating at hotcname[.]help are a reliable pivot. IOCs including Hotejka domains, IPs (62.113.117[.]248, 91.196.33[.]144), affiliate domains (fosetya[.]shop, zylvantrexor[.]lol, goalods[.]lol, trixsolvesxa[.]shop), Cloudflare Pages samples (arrow-berry-gem.pages[.]dev, linen-thorn-wild.pages[.]dev), Telegram handles, and call center numbers are listed in the report.

item.title: AI-Powered Espionage Campaign Targets Government Linux Infrastructure
item.description:
AI-assisted espionage cluster CL-UNK-1211 hit government Linux infrastructure from October 2025 to April 2026, deploying a custom Go RAT, mass web shells, and AI-generated payloads to steal mailboxes and databases while aggressively covering tracks.
Key findings:
- The defining signature of this campaign is AI-assisted payload development. Scripts contained conversational step-by-step reasoning annotations, section headers for faster output parsing, heavy Base64 encoding, and fluid switching between PHP, Python, Bash and JavaScript, all consistent with LLM-generated or AI-agent-deployed code. Unit 42's report includes code snippets showing these inline comments verbatim. Attribution remains unresolved; CL-UNK-1211 is tracked as neither confirmed nation-state nor cybercrime.
- SysGoRAT, a custom cross-platform Go RAT first seen as sys-control-client, beaconed over WebSocket to wss://addr/ws, defaulting to 104.194.158[.]65:443. It supported seven command types including interactive shell, bidirectional proxy relay, and a persist action with six methods: systemd service written to /etc/systemd/system/sys-update.service, crontab entry, Windows Run key at HKCU with binary dropped as %APPDATA%\Onedrive Update\Updater.exe, and a scheduled task named Onedrive. On disk it masqueraded as pip2.7, ea_install, and semanage. C2 infrastructure included 45.88.188[.]140, 198.23.185[.]234, 138.68.244[.]146, 185.21.136[.]6, 72.61.89[.]179, and others listed in the report, alongside domains magento[.]ink, solidmonpe[.]com, and wibu-bau-bawang[.]online.
- Persistence was achieved by hijacking the PHP auto_prepend_file directive across /etc/php/ and /opt/plesk/php/, forcing a malicious web shell at /usr/lib/php/plesk_sys_driver.php to load before every PHP request. Credential harvesting ran on three tracks simultaneously: a .bashrc sudo alias that mimicked the authentication prompt, captured passwords to a log file named Solarwinds.StatusLog.txt, and silently passed input to the real sudo; a PHP injection into a database login page forwarding admin credentials to attacker-controlled storage; and grep sweeps of configuration and history files for cleartext SMTP, email, and database passwords.
- Privilege escalation used LinPEAS for path discovery followed by a PwnKit binary (CVE-2021-4034, hash 44e83f84a5d5219e2f7c3cf1e4f02489cae81361227f46946abe4b8d8245b879) for root. Post-escalation the attackers installed a renamed Python 3 interpreter as .libpython-helper, a SUID shell backdoor as .libsystemd-helper, and a SUID bash copy as .tourch. Lateral movement ran through double-hop XP_CMDSHELL chains across MSSQL servers on separate subnets, sshpass pivoting with hard-coded credentials, and SSH key injection into authorized_keys. GSocket gs-netcat was stored in /dev/shm/.gs-10085/ and executed as [kcached] with parameters hidden in the GSOCKET_ARGS environment variable and HISTFILE=/dev/null to suppress history. A custom Go vulnerability scanner targeting CVE-2025-55182 (React2Shell) was also deployed, with hashes in the report.
- Anti-forensics was systematic. Timestomping via touch -t altered file modification and access times on long-term tools. Single-use scripts were written, executed, and removed in a single command. A mass log wipe targeted authentication, command history, email, OS, web server, and PHP session logs. The attackers then verified their own IP addresses were absent from remaining logs. To mislead analysts, they embedded the string RedTeamOps2025 in scripts and set the password pentest123 on a created account to simulate a red team engagement.
Practitioner takeaway: Start your hunt on PHP configuration files under /etc/php/ and /opt/plesk/php/ for auto_prepend_file pointing to unexpected paths, and check /usr/lib/php/ for anomalous files like plesk_sys_driver.php. Examine .bashrc across all user accounts for sudo aliases or credential-capture functions, and look for a file named Solarwinds.StatusLog.txt or similar masquerades. On Linux persistence, check /etc/systemd/system/ for sys-update.service and crontabs for five-minute entries. For SysGoRAT, hunt binaries named pip2.7, ea_install, or semanage that are not installed by the package manager and establish outbound WebSocket connections on port 443. Review /dev/shm/ for hidden directories and processes presenting as kernel threads ([kcached]). IOCs, hashes, and infrastructure indicators are in the report.

item.title: [0day-rubbish] South River Technologies Titan MFT Server 26.0.0 first-run administrator setup chained to job post-command injection, NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM (8.1)
item.description:
Titan MFT Server 26.0.0 has an unauthenticated first-run setup window chained to post-command injection, reaching NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM. CVSS 3.1 base 8.1 (High); conditionally 9.8 Critical on a confirmed exposed host.
Key findings:
- The chain is two weaknesses linked. CWE-306: while nxUserParams holds zero administrator rows, any network client that reaches port 47443 gets the "Initial Admin User Setup" screen with no token, no CAPTCHA, no IP restriction, and no [Authorize] enforcement, because the entire gate is a single empty-table test in MxSvrParams.cs. CWE-78: the job "Execute After File Transfer Task" field (PostCommandText) is written verbatim to nxJobs and executed by the transfer engine via RunCustomProcessAsync, which reconstructs full cmd.exe shell semantics when the value starts with "cmd", splits on first space otherwise, passes Arguments as a string rather than an ArgumentList vector, and inherits the titanmft.exe service token, which is LocalSystem. No metacharacter rejection, no allow-list, no integrity-level downgrade exists between the write and the process start.
- The attack path is four form submissions and a menu click: create the administrator through the setup screen, authenticate into the management console at /SvrHome/guid/guid, create a job with a post-command such as "cmd /c whoami > marker", and trigger a transfer run. The proof of concept drives the product's own Blazor Server UI through a headless Chromium browser over DevTools protocol; a bare curl or HTTP fetch is not sufficient because the component tree renders only after the circuit boots, meaning a plain GET /Login returns a 3,869-byte shell with none of the setup text, a detection trap that silently reports "not exposed" on a host that is.
- Exposure is a race with deployment, not a permanent condition, which is why 8.1 (AC:H) is the fleet-level score and 9.8 (AC:L) applies only when triaging a specific host already confirmed inside its first-run window. The window opens when the service starts and closes the instant the first administrator account is written. It can reopen after any administrator deletion, database restore, or re-image, because the predicate reads only the row count. The unauthenticated ServerParams response leaks the window-running flag, enabling at-scale enumeration in a single request.
- Detection is artifact-based, not signature-based. The attack leaves no failed logins and no injection payloads. High-signal indicators the report names: the product's own "Post Command: " log line preserving the verbatim command text; any child process of titanmft.exe running as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM (the service has no legitimate reason to spawn shells except administrator-configured post-commands); job-history rows for jobs no schedule references, including successful runs with zero files transferred; and administrator accounts created outside change control with an immediate first-login. Signature hunting, auth-failure monitoring, and SQL-injection or deserialization detection will not fire here.
- Impact on a managed file transfer host is near-worst-case: LocalSystem access exposes every trading partner's exchange credentials, SFTP/FTPS/WebDAV account material, SSH and PGP key material stored in the administration and domain databases, files in transit and at rest across all connector paths, and the host itself as a lateral pivot point. No CVE has been assigned yet; South River Technologies was notified on the same day as publication with no prior coordinated disclosure channel available.
Practitioner takeaway: the authoritative exposure check requires a real browser, not a curl. Load /Login in a browser; "Initial Admin User Setup" with a Create Initial Admin User button means the host is inside the window. From the host, query the row count in the nxUserParams table of the administration SQLite database: zero rows equals exposed, and that check must be repeated after any restore or re-image. Alert on any child process of titanmft.exe and audit every job with a non-empty PostCommandText against change control. If the listener was reachable while the window was open, audit the administrator list, review all job post-commands, and rotate every partner credential and SSH/PGP key the host holds. IOCs, scored CVSS vectors, proof-of-concept modes, and full technical analysis are in the 0day Rubbish report.

item.title: [0day-rubbish] CloudPanel 2.5.4-3 site-settings rootDirectory nginx virtual-host injection to host root code execution (8.8)
item.description:
CloudPanel 2.5.4-3 has a 0day (CVSS 8.8, no CVE yet) letting any authenticated tenant inject nginx directives via the rootDirectory field and reach host uid=0 through the vendor's own root-running nginx and PHP-FPM pool.
- The sink is RootDirectory.php, which composes the rootDirectory value directly into an nginx virtual-host template as root /home/<user>/htdocs/<rootDirectory>; with zero character validation on the web channel. A leading semicolon terminates the legitimate directive, and the attacker's injected blocks land at server context ahead of template location blocks. The vendor's own nginx build ships user root; on line 1 of nginx.conf, and the File Manager PHP-FPM pool declares user = root with no open_basedir, no disable_functions, and no security.limit_extensions. An injected WebDAV block (dav_methods PUT; create_full_put_path on; alias /tmp/;) gives an anonymous file write primitive; a second injected block (root /tmp; fastcgi_pass unix:/run/clp-fm-php-fpm.sock;) gives anonymous PHP execution as root. The identity confirmed over HTTP: uid=0(root) gid=1000(clp). No CVE has been assigned yet; CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H, scored 8.8.
- Exploitation requires ROLE_USER, the lowest panel role, not an administrator. The site-settings handler is not under the admin route prefix and declares only ROLE_USER. Five end-to-end rounds were observed across two reproduction sets, each returning uid=0. Once the settings save lands (a 302 redirect with no error possible, because the reload success check returns true unconditionally), the injected directives are on disk inside a root-owned nginx config file. The two anonymous exploitation steps then require no session at all, so revoking the session or rotating the credential after the save does not stop the second half.
- The full impact on a hosting server: every tenant's document root, SSH keys, the panel SQLite database (password hashes, API tokens), TLS private keys, MariaDB data directory, sudoers, and systemd units are within the achieved boundary. The vendor sudoers drop-in grants the panel account unrestricted passwordless sudo. The save handler logs nothing. A persistent denial-of-service is also possible with no extra work: an invalid payload leaves a broken nginx config with no rollback and no config test on this write path, so the next nginx restart fails while the panel reports success.
- Detection artifacts the report names: a newline, semicolon, or the substrings location, dav_methods, fastcgi_pass, or alias in the root_directory column of the panel database; unexpected growth in /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/*.conf files; any dav_methods directive in those files (shipped templates never emit it); PUT, MKCOL, or PROPFIND verbs in the site-facing access log; new files under /tmp with mode 0600, owned by root, with a .php extension inside 0700 directories; nginx startup messages directive "root" is not terminated by ";" or any emergency message, meaning a poisoned config is already on disk. The product produces no log line for the injection itself.
- Also disclosed alongside, folded into no score: an X-Forwarded-For identity-swap primitive (real_ip trust set to 0.0.0.0/0 with no trusted-proxy configuration in Symfony), silent reload failure, absent nginx config syntax check and rollback on this write path, a static factory application secret identical across installations, a database listener bound to every interface with a hardcoded root password set by the maintainer script, weak non-cryptographic randomness in the password generator called from 17 templates, two anonymous open-redirect conditions, and development artifacts in the release package. No patch exists; the vendor was notified simultaneously with publication and no embargo was agreed.
Treat every ROLE_USER panel account that owns a site as holding host root until a patch ships. Immediately diff /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/ against a known-good baseline, query the panel database for newlines or semicolons in the root_directory column, alert on WebDAV verbs in site access logs, and move the panel listener behind a VPN or source allowlist. The full PoC and technical analysis are at 0day-rubbish[.]com/blog/cloudpanel-site-rootdirectory-nginx-vhost-injection-root-rce and the project archive at github[.]com/Exploit-Garbage/0day-Rubbish.

item.title: ARMORY CASTLE Exploits BeyondTrust
item.description:
Chinese 🇨🇳 APT ARMORY CASTLE (formerly UNC5221) exploited BeyondTrust Remote Support as a zero-day in late August 2026, deploying two new custom malware families and achieving host-level root access with credential vault extraction.
- CVE-2026-102764 is an unauthenticated file upload vulnerability affecting all BeyondTrust Remote Support versions up to 26.2.3. ARMORY CASTLE exploited it as a zero-day weeks before today's disclosure, giving them arbitrary file write on appliances and a path to full host compromise. Exploitation evidence lives in the access, syslog, messages, thin-scc, brain, and SSL log files inside the LUKS-encrypted /home partition. Those logs are your primary forensic source, and the actor knew it: they systematically deleted /ns/log/auth.log, /ns/log/ssl.log, /ns/log/http-access.log, /var/log/messages, /home/%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT%/ingredi/log/httpd_access.log, and more than a dozen other paths. item.title: linux kernel: PwnEscape: Guest-to-Host KVM Escape (CVE-2026-99999)
item.description:
CVE-2026-99999: A deferred-checksum TOCTOU flaw in the Linux kernel networking stack enables guest-controlled metadata to rewrite IPv4 headers after validation, producing host-memory disclosure and, in a controlled lab chain, full KVM guest-to-host escape.
Key details:
- The root cause is a trust-inversion in CHECKSUM_PARTIAL handling. A guest can supply skb->csum_start and skb->csum_offset values that pass the initial virtio/TUN admission check but are not re-validated against the network header after L2 decapsulation. In ip_do_fragment(), the historical code called skb_checksum_help() before refreshing the IPv4 header pointer, allowing the deferred write to mutate the ihl field from 0x45 (IHL=5, 20-byte header) to 0x4f (IHL=15, 60-byte header) while the version nibble stays intact. Later consumers trust the mutated interpretation as authoritative.
- The memory disclosure is concrete and bounded. With skb_headlen(skb) = 28 bytes (20-byte IPv4 header + 8 bytes of payload), the manipulated fragmenter treats the next 40 bytes as IPv4 options. Eight are inside legitimate linear packet data; the trailing 32 bytes are host kernel memory the guest never provided. The fragmenter then emits those bytes in outgoing IP option fields, turning an internal read into an externally observable artifact on the wire. The researchers confirmed this produced 32 bytes of host-memory disclosure per active case, reproducible across Linux 6.12 and 7.x.
- The researchers escalated beyond read-only disclosure in their own owned KVM fixture, demonstrating selected 64-byte host-kernel writes and a bounded host-root execution chain confirmed across four cold boots. Part 2, covering the write primitive and the path from disclosure to host control, is not yet published. The report explicitly states the authors expect exploits in weaker hypervisor configurations within weeks and in default configurations within a month.
- The accepted fix, commit 6785011f8b16 ("ipv4: validate checksum_start before completing checksum"), adds a shared helper ip_check_csum_start() to include/net/ip.h and places it before skb_checksum_help() in five IPv4 checksum-completion consumers. The invariant enforced is: skb->csum_start >= skb->network_header + ip_hdrlen(skb). The commit message explicitly describes this as defense-in-depth; broader ingress validation of virtio/TUN checksum metadata is listed as further work. The patch landed in net.git on October 8 and merged into Linus's tree October 14, 2026. Stable backports and formal CVE publication are ongoing.
- This is not a KVM hypervisor bug. The vulnerable component is the host Linux networking stack, reachable from any guest workload that can influence virtio or TUN checksum metadata. The researchers name the attack class deferred-metadata trust inversion: untrusted metadata is validated against an early packet representation, the packet is transformed, and a deferred write then modifies security-relevant bytes that later consumers treat as already trusted. The audit question this raises for reviewers is: after every packet transformation, can a deferred writer still reach bytes whose semantic meaning the kernel has already consumed?
For responders and kernel maintainers: check whether your distribution has backported 6785011f8b16 or carries an equivalent guard; stable backport status is not confirmed at time of writing. If you run multi-tenant KVM, container, or sandbox workloads on Linux hosts, treat this as actively being weaponized. At the kernel audit level, the pattern to hunt is any path where sk_buff checksum metadata crosses a trust boundary (virtio_net, TUN, AF_PACKET) and is consumed by a deferred operation without a post-normalization network-header bounds check. The report's public netdev patch series and commit diff contain the source-level rationale for all five affected consumer sites.
