item.title: [0day-rubbish] Synametrics Syncrify 6.2 build 1178 authenticated PublicLink chunk-upload path traversal to /etc/cron.d and root command execution (7.5)
item.description:
Synametrics Syncrify 6.2 build 1178 has an unpatched path traversal in its chunk-upload handler, letting an authenticated backup user write to /etc/cron.d and achieve root command execution. No CVE assigned yet; CVSS 3.1 base score 7.5 (conditionally 8.8).
- The flaw lives in the PublicLink handler at operation=pb&st=u. The binary framing bypasses all HTTP parameter parsing, so the attacker-controlled filename field is passed directly into new File(base, filename) with no separator rejection, no ".." check, and no canonical containment test. A chunk name of ../../../../../etc/cron.d/backdoor exits the per-user PublicLinks folder, and a mkdirs() call creates any missing parent on the way. The service process runs as uid=0, confirmed by file ownership and scheduler output, so the written fragment is accepted by cron as a root-authored job and executes on the next minute boundary. Three sibling handlers in the same codebase all implement the missing check; this branch simply omits it.
- Authentication is required but set low. The handler authenticates against the backup-user store (config/UserMappings.xml), not the admin store. The session is server-side so it cannot be forged. PR:L in the CVSS reflects that any provisioned backup user, the product's lowest-trust account type, is sufficient. The password-recovery operation on the unauthenticated surface is a CWE-203 enumeration weakness only, and no unauthenticated write or execution route was found across all 47 level-0 operations examined.
- For defenders, application logs are a dead end. The upload branch returns the identical code="1" reply for a traversing name and a legitimate one, produces no rejection, and logs no path decision. The detection signal the report identifies is behavioral: an authenticate-then-upload-one-or-two-small-chunks pattern with no further protocol activity deviates from a genuine backup session's long request sequence. Filesystem integrity monitoring on /etc/cron.d, /etc/crontab, /var/spool/cron, init unit directories, and the service's own binary and config paths is the reliable control. Alert specifically on any new file in a scheduler directory whose content includes a user field of root.
- Impact extends well beyond shell access. Root on this host means read access to every repository for every configured backup client (a cross-tenant confidentiality breach), plaintext or reversibly-permuted credentials from the backup-user store, and integrity control over the backup chain itself. Persistence is structural: the cron fragment recurs on every minute boundary until deleted and survives both service and host restarts. One successful chunk write is enough.
- No patch exists at time of disclosure. The vendor has no security.txt and no published disclosure policy; Synametrics was notified on the day of publication. The report also notes the same sradef framework underpins sibling products including SynaMan, and the shared lib4njre.jar is common to all of them, making the same construction worth auditing across that family.
Practitioner action: audit /etc/cron.d and the Syncrify PublicLinks tree (opt/Syncrify/PublicLinks) now for unexpected files. Review config/UserMappings.xml for accounts without a corresponding client deployment. Until a patch ships, move the portal listener to a management network, run the service under an unprivileged account where repository ownership permits it (removing the /etc/cron.d escalation while the write primitive survives), and maintain an offline or immutable copy of repositories outside the server's own write reach.

item.title: [0day-rubbish] Abyss Web Server X1 2.16.22.0 first-run console credential takeover to configuration-write log-as-CGI command execution (7.5)
item.description:
Abyss Web Server X1 2.16.22.0 has a zero-day chain: unauthenticated credential creation during first-run, then log-poisoning-as-CGI delivers OS command execution. No CVE assigned yet, CVSS 3.1 scored 7.5 High (AV:A), rising to 9.8 Critical if the console reaches a public network.
- The chain has two co-equal roots, CWE-306 and CWE-78, and neither fix alone breaks it. During the first-run window, before any console password exists, a POST to /console/credentials with no credentials mints a new administrator. The moment that POST succeeds the window closes and the same endpoint returns 401, so the attacker's own request locks out the legitimate operator. The window re-opens on every redeployment from a pristine config, every container restart from a clean image, and every operator-documented password-recovery procedure that removes the credential nodes, making this a recurring surface, not a one-time race.
- Three authenticated configuration writes then convert the logging plane into an execution plane. POST to /hosts/host@0/edit/scripting/paths/path@0/edit sets vpath=/ with type=0, placing the entire virtual path space under CGI scope. POST to /hosts/host@0/edit/log points the access log at an arbitrary absolute path inside the document root, with no whitelist and a built-in file browser that walks from the filesystem root to aid discovery. POST to /hosts/host@0/edit/scripting/interpreters/interpreter@0/edit binds /bin/sh as the interpreter for the extension log. A POST to / with restart=Restart applies all three.
- Payload delivery requires no file upload. A request whose User-Agent is zz"; (command); # is logged in combined format, where the double-quote closes the format field, the semicolon separates a shell statement, and the trailing comment discards the remainder. A subsequent anonymous GET on the log path triggers /bin/sh against the log file as a CGI child. Confirmation is server-side: cgi.log records CGI: [/bin/sh x.log] URI: /x.log and the shell emits line N: 127.0.0.1: command not found as it re-executes every prior log line. The trigger request itself returns 500 because /bin/sh writes no CGI headers. The research team observed uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root) in a marker file on their verified instance, though root is explicitly tied to their use of --allow-root and is not claimed as the universal default.
- Detection is structurally weak because every request in the chain is legitimate documented product usage: setup form, authenticated config POSTs, restart button, a 404 with an unusual User-Agent, and an anonymous 500 on a document-root file. The highest-fidelity signals are: cgi.log entries naming a non-script file (a shell invoked on a .log path), 500 responses for paths ending in .log, .txt, .tmp, or .bak, configuration audit hits on a vpath=/ CGI scope entry, an interpreter whose file is a shell, or a log file element pointing inside the document root. Access-log lines whose User-Agent contains shell metacharacters (";, #, $(, redirections) are the payload signature and rare in benign traffic. Repeated unauthenticated GET /console/ probes from many hosts indicate active window surveying, since an unarmed instance returns a distinctive 302 while an armed instance returns 401.
- No CVE has been assigned. No patch exists. Aprelium has been notified via their published support mailbox. The Attack Vector is Adjacent because the console's default ipcontrol block permits all RFC1918 ranges and IPv6 ULA/link-local while refusing public addresses, but that still covers every office LAN, home LAN, shared management VLAN, container bridge network, and cloud VPC subnet. Conditional scores reach 8.8 High if the window is left open indefinitely (automation that never arms, containers rebuilt from pristine images) and 9.8 Critical if port 9999 is published through NAT or a same-host reverse proxy.
Until a patch exists: arm the console in the same automation step that installs the server and never skip it on redeployment. Bind or firewall port 9999 to loopback. Audit abyss.conf for a vpath=/ CGI scope entry, an interpreter file pointing to any shell, and a log file element inside the document root. Watch cgi.log for shell invocations on data-extension files. Run the server without --allow-root using CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE or a port redirect instead. A Python standard-library proof-of-concept is published in the 0day Rubbish repository at the path named in the advisory.

item.title: [0day-rubbish] Auerswald COMmander 6000 / 6000R 8.6D unauthenticated provisioning import zip-slip to root binary hijack and root code execution (9.8)
item.description:
Zero-day CVSS 9.8: Auerswald COMmander 6000/6000R PBX hands unauthenticated attackers root in two HTTP requests, exposing SIP credentials, voicemail, and call records for every extension the appliance serves. No CVE assigned yet, no patch exists.
Technical breakdown:
- The attack is a two-hop chain. Hop 1 hits /provisioning_data_import with no cookie and no credential. The handler stores the uploaded file and then calls the bundled miniunz extractor (md5: 36eb80de5ac55a8bbfc31e77c1d10e3d) as root with the -o overwrite flag. Because neither the application nor miniunz validates archive entry names, an entry path of ../../../opt/auerswald/hping2 escapes the extraction directory and overwrites that root-owned mode-0755 binary with attacker-supplied bytes. The original permission bits survive the truncating write, so the replacement is immediately executable with no chmod needed.
- Hop 2 hits /netdiagnostic_execute, also unauthenticated. The diagnostics handler runs /bin/sh -c "/opt/auerswald/hping2 -1 -I eth0 -c 3 [target] -p [port]" as root. The target argument is correctly whitelisted to 0-9A-Za-z.-:/, but the path /opt/auerswald/hping2 is a compile-time constant: the kernel reads the attacker's shebang, executes the payload as uid=0, and returns stdout directly in the HTTP response body. No out-of-band channel is required.
- The authorization failure is systemic, not incidental. The vendor FastCGI application registers 750 named routes; the session and credential evaluator covers only 12 of them. Both /provisioning_data_import and /netdiagnostic_execute are declared AccessLevel 2 and return HTTP 200 to requests carrying no Cookie and no Authorization header. The report sampled more than 40 other routes during mapping, each returning live configuration or performing state changes unauthenticated. The same packet-capture handler registered at three route names returns 200 at level 2 and 401 at levels 4 and 6, which shows authorization is attached to route families, not to the operations they expose.
- The application runs as uid=0 from init and never drops privilege. The rootfs ships no suid or sgid binary, so there is no privilege boundary between the web layer and the telephony stack. Root on the PBX means the SIP stack, trunk credentials, extension passwords, voicemail, call detail records, and the auto-provisioning templates that configure the entire managed handset fleet. The configuration database at /data/db/ contains fields including cryptPasswd, passwd, AdminPasswdHash, and remote_access_token; user certificate private keys sit under /data/certs/user-certs. Firmware and init script paths are writable, making persistence across update cycles feasible. The report also notes 17 additional unauthenticated defects in the same firmware build disclosed alongside this one, including a root packet-capture stream returned directly to the caller.
- The advisory's detection section is worth reading carefully because the chain produces no failed login, no 401, and no privilege-change event. The product's own log records a normal diagnostics command because the command string is ordinary. What is detectable: /opt/auerswald/hping2 becoming a small text file instead of its known 74,376-byte binary (md5: afc33cdf96b060e636c463e622b6ae1b); root-owned mode-0666 files appearing outside /data/provisioning; a /bin/sh child process whose command names /opt/auerswald/hping2; and an unauthenticated client POSTing to /provisioning_data_import followed by /netdiagnostic_execute. The overwrite persists on flash until the binary is restored, so the two requests need not be temporally adjacent and correlation by proximity is unreliable.
If you operate or protect one of these appliances: verify the digest of /opt/auerswald/hping2 and /opt/auerswald/minizip/miniunz against the values above right now and alert on any size reduction or zero-length file. Restrict the management listener to a dedicated VLAN or named administration hosts immediately, this chain needs nothing but network reachability. If compromise is suspected, re-verify the entire /opt tree and all init scripts under /opt/auerswald/scripts/run-*, then rotate every credential the device holds: administrator accounts, extension passwords, SIP trunk credentials, LDAP bind credentials, syslog credentials, and device certificates. A public Python PoC using only the standard library is in the report repository.

item.title: [0day-rubbish] PacsOne Server 7.3.9 authenticated DICOMweb STOW-RS SOP Instance UID path traversal to www-data code execution on a PACS host (7.2)
item.description:
Unpatched path traversal in PacsOne Server 7.3.9 lets an authenticated user write arbitrary PHP into the served web tree, achieving code execution as www-data on a medical imaging host containing patient DICOM data.
Key findings:
- The flaw sits in import() inside dicomweb.php (approx. lines 1391-1440). The DICOMweb STOW-RS handler stowrs.php reads the SOP Instance UID (0008,0018) from the posted DICOM object via RawTags::getAttr(), applies only trim(), and passes the raw value directly into a rename() call: $newfile = $dir . "/" . uid. A UID of ../../../php/x.php moves the file out of the study directory and into the Apache-served /pacsone tree. The product already contains isUidValid() and already calls it on the unauthenticated wadoAnonymized.php read path, where its character whitelist blocks "/". The store path never calls it. CVSS:3.1 7.2 High (AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H); a conditional 8.8 applies if a non-administrator account holds the stowrs privilege, which the researchers did not demonstrate but flag as realistic for modality or partner-PACS deployments.
- The 128-byte DICOM preamble is ignored by the parser, so it can carry a PHP stub. rename() executes before the database inserts, meaning the write is not transactional: a deliberately incomplete object (missing Patient Name or Patient ID) triggers the failure branch's unlink($newfile) on the attacker-chosen path and returns HTTP 409 with failure reason 272, while a complete object returns HTTP 200 and leaves a 580-byte, mode 0600 file owned by www-data. Execution is then confirmed by an unauthenticated GET to the written file path, because the access gate covers the store operation but not the file it created.
- On a PACS host, www-data owns the DICOM study repository. Demonstrated impact includes arbitrary file write into the served PHP tree, code execution at that identity, and consequent read access to stored DICOM objects (which carry patient name, ID, birth date, referring physician, institution, and imaging data in their headers), the PHP configuration file holding the installer-configured database credentials, and the full relational schema including user accounts and the privilege table. No patient data was accessed in the research; the chain also supports integrity impact (altering or fabricating studies) and availability impact (disrupting the Apache worker or the study browser). No CVE has been assigned yet; no patch exists.
- Detection opportunities named in the report: query the database for image.path LIKE '%../%' or image.uuid LIKE '%/%' (the product stores the uncanonicalised path, making this possible). In the Apache access log, look for a POST to stowrs.php followed within seconds by GETs to a .php path that did not previously exist, especially with a response body containing binary DICOM bytes after any command output. That binary tail is the tell. File-integrity monitoring over the served PHP tree will catch the mode 0600 file. Signals that will NOT fire: nothing in DICOM upper-layer logs, no anomalous STOW-RS response status on a successful run (it is HTTP 200), no sudo or privilege-change audit event.
Practitioner takeaway: if you operate or protect a PacsOne installation, run the database query for image.path LIKE '%../%' immediately and audit every row in the privilege table with stowrs=1. Treat each such credential as equivalent to a shell on the imaging host. Restrict stowrs.php, wadors.php, and qidors.php at the proxy or firewall to known modality and partner addresses. If the traversal shows evidence of use, treat the full stored study repository on that host as readable by the attacker and handle it as an imaging-archive exposure under your breach-notification obligations. The written PHP file persists until manually removed and is reachable unauthenticated; rotating the PACS credential does not remove it, and its execution does not appear in STOW-RS logs.

item.title: YuanKong RAT: the Android remote-control service that stamps its operators' names into every build
item.description:
YuanKong RAT is a Chinese-language, multi-tenant Android banking RAT that bakes every operator's account handle into the compiled DEX, so tearing down one build statically recovers the roster of all 42 operators without ever touching the C2.
- The Nova dropper (com.system.loader.va363d031, signer af92f7d616564dabffb0679a1a38fb24d6a6c4e4a90114c6eb0834c57dd456c9, O=Nova OU=APK Factory C=SG) stores its own decryption key and IV in cleartext at assets/vault-config.json. The payload is a "SVLT-XOR-v2" blob: a simple two-key XOR over a SVLT-magic container, reversible with a few lines of Python from the config alone. The decrypted ZIP contains the child APK. No key derivation, no server round-trip, no anti-analysis gate.
- Every child payload across 110 droppers and 57 distinct builds is signed by one shared certificate: 73cbe8e3730cacfdd208f22eab468bb5495a78c0eb2cb37eff5af0cafe321387 (O=YuanKong, CN=Remote Control, L=Beijing, C=CN, valid to 2053). Package names and build brands rotate every build (echorelay, atlaswave, fluxlink, zenithwave, etc.) but the signer never changes. This certificate is the family anchor.
- Operator identity is compiled in as DEX string constants, not fetched from the server. The config class exposes apkAccountId (e.g. account_mulcetn2_9d226b242cac), apkAccountName (e.g. lichunfeng7), and a six-digit enrollment code (e.g. 863456). Every foreground-app beacon sent over the Socket.IO/WebSocket channel to apppanda[.]xyz, ktxapp[.]com, ktx123[.]net, and 206.82.1[.]14 includes all three fields plus apkOwnerSource = "apk build". The RAT reports the operator to the C2 and to anyone who can read the wire or the binary.
- Credential and PIN theft operates entirely through the accessibility tree and screen capture, with no SMS, contacts, call-log, camera, or microphone permissions. The child screen-captures and live-streams (MediaProjection or, after escalation, screenrecord over the local ADB shell delivering H.264), reads every text-field edit as a KeyInputRecord (TYPE_VIEW_TEXT_CHANGED: appPackage, beforeText, afterText, inputField), reconstructs device PINs from tap coordinates mapped against a digit-button layout cached from the accessibility tree, and overlays operator-supplied HTML for payment-PIN phishing. Captured records queue in a Room database (MonitorDatabase: PaymentPinRecord, KeyInputRecord, TouchRecord) and flush as delta messages so a socket drop loses nothing.
- Local privilege escalation uses the device's own adbd against itself. The app enables Wireless Debugging via Settings[.]Global through accessibility, scrapes the six-digit pairing code and port from the system pairing dialog by walking the accessibility node tree (accepting matches on resource-id or on a regex pattern), pairs via libadb-android SPAKE2 (HKDF-SHA256 to an AES-128-GCM session key derived at runtime, never stored), connects to 127.0.0.1:5555, and runs pm grant WRITE_SECURE_SETTINGS plus drops /data/local/tmp/remote_control_daemon.sh, a shell loop that writes -1000 to /proc/pid/oom_score_adj to make the RAT unkillable. This escalates to shell UID 2000, not root, and the same tradecraft appears in RedHook (Pradeo, July 2026) and RatHat (Zimperium, September 2026), making it an emerging Android pattern.
Hunt on the shared child certificate 73cbe8e3730cacfdd208f22eab468bb5495a78c0eb2cb37eff5af0cafe321387 in your mobile threat pipeline: it survives every package-name and brand rotation and ties all 57 confirmed payloads together. Block or alert on outbound WebSocket connections to ktxapp[.]com, ktx123[.]net, and 206.82.1[.]14. On any collected sample, static extraction of apkAccountId, apkAccountName, and the enrollment code from the DEX config class (k4.l3 or its obfuscated equivalent) gives you the operator without network access. The full IOC table and 42-operator account roster are in the STAR Labs report.

item.title: [0day-rubbish] Maian Pal 2.1 product image upload with no extension allow-list to PHP webshell and www-data uid 33 code execution (7.2, PR:H)
item.description:
Maian Pal 2.1 PHP shopping cart ships with no extension allow-list on its product image upload path, letting an authenticated admin drop a webshell directly into the served document tree and execute OS commands as www-data. No CVE assigned yet, no vendor patch available.
Technical breakdown:
- The flaw lives in products::pictures() at class.products.php lines 333-410. The stored filename is derived from the client-supplied value via a single ternary: when the shipped default thumbcfg() setting 'rename' => 'no' is active, $picPath = $name, giving the attacker full control over the filename including extension. move_uploaded_file() runs before any image validation, so a .php file lands on disk intact at content/products/<ID>/<filename>.php before getimagesize() is even called. When getimagesize() fails on a PHP file, the switch falls through to a suppressed [@]copy(), producing a tmb_-prefixed sibling. Neither object is unlinked. The application returns {"status":"ok"} either way.
- Execution is guaranteed by a second, independent gap. content/products/ sits inside the document root, carries no Apache deny file (contrast: admin/import/ ships with "Deny from all"), and the front-controller RewriteCond checks !-f, so a file that exists on disk bypasses the rewrite and is handed directly to the PHP handler. The exploit chain is two requests: one POST to /admin/index.php?ajax-ops=add creates the object and the response body itself returns the product ID, making the final URL fully predictable. One GET to /content/products/<ID>/<name>.php?cmd=<command> executes it.
- Turning on the rename='yes' option does not close the chain. That branch generates a server-side stem but still appends the extension via strrchr(name, '.'), so a .php upload still produces an executable file with a server-chosen name. The advisory argues this from the assignment expression rather than a dynamic run and is explicit about that distinction. A deployment that switched this knob thinking it was protected is not.
- Impact at www-data is higher than the context normally implies for a shopping cart host. The service account must read control/_cfg.php to function, so code execution immediately yields the database credentials, SECRET_KEY, the administrator credential material, and any stored payment-gateway, PayPal, mail, or API keys. The 32 installed tables include customer accounts in shop_accounts, orders, and addresses. Financial data is writable: prices, stock levels, discount rules, and order contents are database rows, and modifications travel over the application's own database connection, invisible in the HTTP access log. The webshell itself persists across session expiry, service restarts, and application updates, and a cleanup that removes only the named object leaves the tmb_-prefixed sibling. CVSS 3.1 base score is 7.2 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H). No CVE identifier has been assigned.
- The advisory was disclosed unconditionally after Maian Media was notified through its support mailbox. No security.txt, no VDP, and no pre-publication intake channel existed for this product. No patch exists at time of disclosure.
Practitioner takeaway: No vendor fix is available, so the immediate actions are operational. Inventory content/products/*/ right now for any non-image extension files and for tmb_-prefixed objects sharing a non-image basename: remove both halves of every pair. Treat any .php, .phtml, or .phar file in that tree as an active webshell. In your web server config, add an execution restriction to content/products/ independent of .htaccess (SetHandler none, php_admin_flag engine off, or the nginx equivalent) so the protection survives AllowOverride None. Add an edge or WAF rule alerting on GET requests matching ^/content/products/.*\.ph(p[3457]?|t|ml|ar)$ with a query string. If compromise is suspected, treat the full contents of control/_cfg.php, including the database credentials, SECRET_KEY, administrator credential, and all payment-gateway and API keys, as disclosed and rotate all of them. Assume database contents were readable. The advisory and proof-of-concept are published at the 0day-rubbish[.]com blog and the Exploit-Garbage GitHub repository.

- Turning on the rename='yes' option does not close the chain. That branch generates a server-side stem but still appends the extension via strrchr(name, '.'), so a .php upload still produces an executable file with a server-chosen name. The advisory argues this from the assignment expression rather than a dynamic run and is explicit about that distinction. A deployment that switched this knob thinking it was protected is not.

- Impact at www-data is higher than the context normally implies for a shopping cart host. The service account must read control/_cfg.php to function, so code execution immediately yields the database credentials, SECRET_KEY, the administrator credential material, and any stored payment-gateway, PayPal, mail, or API keys. The 32 installed tables include customer accounts in shop_accounts, orders, and addresses. Financial data is writable: prices, stock levels, discount rules, and order contents are database rows, and modifications travel over the application's own database connection, invisible in the HTTP access log. The webshell itself persists across session expiry, service restarts, and application updates, and a cleanup that removes only the named object leaves the tmb_-prefixed sibling. CVSS 3.1 base score is 7.2 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H). No CVE identifier has been assigned.

- The advisory was disclosed unconditionally after Maian Media was notified through its support mailbox. No security.txt, no VDP, and no pre-publication intake channel existed for this product. No patch exists at time of disclosure.

Practitioner takeaway: No vendor fix is available, so the immediate actions are operational. Inventory content/products/*/ right now for any non-image extension files and for tmb_-prefixed objects sharing a non-image basename: remove both halves of every pair. Treat any .php, .phtml, or .phar file in that tree as an active webshell. In your web server config, add an execution restriction to content/products/ independent of .htaccess (SetHandler none, php_admin_flag engine off, or the nginx equivalent) so the protection survives AllowOverride None. Add an edge or WAF rule alerting on GET requests matching ^/content/products/.*\.ph(p[3457]?|t|ml|ar)$ with a query string. If compromise is suspected, treat the full contents of control/_cfg.php, including the database credentials, SECRET_KEY, administrator credential, and all payment-gateway and API keys, as disclosed and rotate all of them. Assume database contents were readable. The advisory and proof-of-concept are published at the 0day-rubbish[.]com blog and the Exploit-Garbage GitHub repository.

item.title: Ivanti Connect Secure Zero-Day CVE-2026-104935 Exploited in Chained Attacks
item.description:
CVE-2026-104935: UTA0576 chains three Ivanti Connect Secure zero-days to reach root on a fully patched appliance, stealing credentials and sniffing internal traffic. Patch is partial: the privilege escalation flaw has no fix yet.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-104935 (CVSS 8.6, CWE-290) covers an auth bypass in /dana-na/auth/url_default/welcome.cgi and a race-condition RCE in the wu.cgi upload handler. The bypass works by sending an X-DSCGI-PATH header pointing at a protected CGI script, routing an unauthenticated request to code that should sit behind login. The RCE exploits a window between file write and validation: a Perl script uploaded with a .zip extension is raced and executed before the appliance deletes it. The third flaw, an unpatched privilege escalation through in-memory patching of libdsplibs[.]so and DSCache abuse, elevates the cgi-server session to root. No web shell, no persistent malware: every command re-ran the full chain and returned output in the HTTP response, leaving almost nothing on disk.
- UTA0576 post-exploitation was systematic and hands-on-keyboard. Custom LDAP tools (/tmp/ml.py, /tmp/rq5.py) queried Active Directory for LAPS passwords and BitLocker recovery keys using the appliance's own AD service account. A renamed tcpdump binary masquerading as dsstatmond ran from a hidden /data/.icscap/ directory, writing eight rotating capture files. /data/.icscap/h.py parsed cap0 for TCP 389 traffic to extract plaintext LDAP credentials, HTTP Basic credentials, and NTLM challenge-response material. /tmp/mk.py included Kerberoasting functionality. A password-spraying script (sp_run.py) produced spray_hits.json. All exfiltration ran back over the exploit channel itself.
- Anti-forensics were deliberate and layered. Selective log entries were removed from /home/runtime/dlogs/debuglog and /var/log/audit/audit.log. The in-memory libdsplibs[.]so patch and DSCache modification were both reversed through /proc/self/mem after use. Temporary files and the root Perl payload were self-deleted. Because of this cleanup, Volexity and Ivanti had to reconstruct the chain from memory images, disk images, and core dumps. Memory analysis surfaced the dsstatmond sniffer at PID 5012 and recovered actor scripts, JSON output, and PCAP files that were gone from disk.
- CVE-2026-104935 is listed in CISA KEV as of October 13, 2026. The patched versions are 25.1.1.2, 25.1.3.0/25.1.3.1, and 22.8R2.5. Versions 22.7.x and below are not affected. The privilege escalation step is still unpatched. The 22.7 and 22.8 code lines reach end of life January 31, 2027. Ivanti found part of the flaw internally in June 2026 but held it for a regular release, and active exploitation began by early October. One researcher warned that the trivial bypass and repeatable race condition make widespread exploitation likely as others study the patches.
- Ivanti's Integrity Checker Tool does not detect this chain because all library patching happens in memory and all DSCache changes are restored. CISA issued the same warning explicitly. A clean integrity check result does not rule out compromise on an appliance running ICS 22.8R2.4 or earlier affected versions.
Practitioner takeaway: Do not stop at patching, and do not trust the Integrity Checker. Hunt welcome.cgi access logs for high request volumes and for any request where X-DSCGI-PATH does not match the URL path, including paths to wu.cgi or /home/runtime/tmp/. Check /tmp/ for ml[.]py, rq5[.]py, mk[.]py, rr[.]py, pu.txt, sp_run.py, and related files. Look for a dsstatmond process or a hidden .icscap directory under /data/. Audit /home/runtime/dlogs/debuglog and /var/log/audit/audit.log for continuity gaps. On any appliance you suspect, collect memory before you do anything else: the evidence chain lives there. Treat every credential stored on or captured by a potentially exposed appliance as compromised, including domain accounts used for LDAP, LAPS material, and BitLocker keys. The C2 IP 108.165.147[.]64 (Evoxt VPS) was observed running OpenVPN September 30 through October 7, 2026. The complete indicator set is in a public repository linked from Volexity's report.

item.title: How RL mapped a Midnight Blizzard-linked campaign from two hashes
item.description:
Russian 🇷🇺 Midnight Blizzard-linked operator GTG-20006 rebuilt AI-flagged implants five times in 25 days. ReversingLabs turned two published hashes into a 12-server, 61-domain campaign map through five telemetry pivots that neither Anthropic nor Microsoft's reports contained.
Key findings:
- The two seed samples are ChocoShell (SHA-256: be99857449d2856dd5a84e21c8a3d5e0e01456adb44062ddec5a6b4970d8d42c, PowerShell stager, 54.6 KB) and CornFlake (SHA-256: 918fa52ae45ed60ba7cc8bdc99c3cbe9ab92e0375ec31fc05d0d4513be11c593, Go x64 backdoor, 7.7 MB). RL first observed them on July 6 and July 10, 2026, weeks before Microsoft published on July 31 and Anthropic on September 10. The stager beacons to 213.145.86[.]112 via HTTPS requests to /t/pixel[.]gif with query labels stage2_entry and stage2_ctx_, exfiltrates via POST to /t/event, and collects browser credentials including a Chrome App-Bound Encryption bypass. The backdoor copies itself to %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\svchost32\svchost32.exe, writes an HKCU Run value, instantiates a Schedule.Service COM object, injects into a suspended process, reads Edge, Chrome, Firefox and Teams cache data, and produced a keylogger YARA hit in sandbox (T1056.001, T1055.012, T1547.001, T1053.005).
- A YARA retro-hunt keyed on the beacon path and the operator-chosen stage labels, not the hash, returned seven malicious PowerShell files and zero goodware. Five are rebuilt stagers with different hashes but an identical 35-item capability profile and the same ATT&CK tactic distribution (Defense Evasion 6, Discovery 4, Execution 4). ssdeep splits them into two variants: the Anthropic-listed stager groups with SHA-1s 154d8cfd9e304b6644216456759b7fd12daf85c1, 1b97e0df9600335b0cd8db2eb4577d3dbf6e76db, 7acb7082d37854877a08999374460c9d7e5cd663, and 99f2eac2f00451a9a55521905add54205e336b9d at scores of 88-100, while 04b64591837c5c2696c2a4423b1bb3dab00a0f01 and seventh match 6e5c658261f72fda92d475ac96f0213159af785d pair only with each other at 82. The operator made code changes large enough to break fuzzy similarity while preserving every operational behavior.
- Two 60-byte Windows Internet Shortcut (.url) lure files (SHA-256: 5bc3c615da8dd7ef45e421d26a97644679ba0a0647b24efc96ebed8348f403d2 and 92cf0b883d220ba37f5ab378920fefdfdddc4fa76ee6c046696a7e5853a95c33) open stager download paths on the staging server, first seen July 14 and 17. None of 37 antivirus engines flagged either file, and RL's cloud verdict was still goodware on September 28, because they contain no code. Their malice is entirely in where they point. This is a detection gap worth understanding: a .url file pointing to a raw-IP HTTPS path with a session token is the infection chain's user-facing step and invisible to AV consensus.
- The phishing infrastructure targets Ukraine 🇺🇦 and European government, diplomatic, think-tank and defense-industrial organizations using M365 lookalikes (ms365-live[.]com, owa-ms365[.]com, ms365-device[.]com, m365-owa[.]com), a WhatsApp Web pairing lure (wa-meeting[.]com), and institution-specific lookalikes including chathamhouse[.]eu and chamber-ua[.]org. As of October 5, 2026, the staging server at 213.145.86[.]112 still answered HTTP 200 on /s and served a malicious file. Four of five analyzed phishing domains remained live. Median third-party reputation flagging across 61 malicious domains: 2 of 47 sources. The staging server sat at 1 source before Microsoft published.
- An unresolved hunting lead: RL relationship data places the Go backdoor under "Files Communicating with IP" for 192.142.52[.]31 (Ultahost, Madrid, RL first seen 2026-09-06, 2 of 50 sources, no classification). Three additional files also reference it. It appears in neither Anthropic's nor Microsoft's report. Validate before blocking.
Practitioner takeaway: Two YARA rules (RL_MidnightBlizzard_GTG20006_PowerShell_PixelBeacon_2026 and RL_MidnightBlizzard_GTG20006_Go_Svchost32_Backdoor_2026) and two Sigma rules, one hunting process creation from %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\svchost32\svchost32.exe (Sigma id: 7c1d4e2a-5b8f-4a3e-9d61-2f0b8c7e4a19) and one hunting PowerShell Script Block Logging for the raw-IP pixel.gif beacon pattern with stage2_entry or stage2_ctx_ (Sigma id: 3e9a7f10-8c2d-4b6e-a5f1-6d0c9b2e7a44, requires Script Block Logging enabled), are published in the report alongside the full IOC set on GitHub. Validate YARA rules against a goodware corpus before production: the Go rule's module combination appears in legitimate Go service agents and depends on the svchost32 strings to discriminate.

item.title: ROMULUS: Analysis of a New Multi-Payload ClickFix Delivery Platform
item.description:
ROMULUS is a multi-payload ClickFix delivery platform serving at least two distinct malware chains, one via trojanized MSI and DLL sideloading, the other dropping LegionLoader through a nested encrypted archive with an artificially inflated 882 GB PE.
Key findings:
- ROMULUS is a shared cybercriminal delivery backend, not a single campaign. Forescout identified six IPs exposing the same dark-themed login panel (96.62.224[.]81, 86.109.75[.]7, 151.240.151[.]223, 23.94.145[.]224, 93.152.224[.]118, 2.27.248[.]127) via VirusTotal entity:url title:"Romulus" path:"/login" and Shodan http.title:"Romulus". The panel tracks "unique installs" and "all runs" with per-country breakdowns, a live counter, and a 14-day timeline, functioning as an operator dashboard. Tokens are 12-character hex strings appended to /s/ (PowerShell staging scripts) and /app/ (trojanized MSI files), allowing the backend to serve different payloads per campaign or victim.
- Route A (T1574.002, T1218.007) replays the Stardock DeElevation chain Huntress documented. A PowerShell stager downloads IconEdit2Turb.msi from hxxp://86.109.75[.]7/app/19481b28bd67/IconEdit2Turb.msi using a Chrome/131 user-agent over TLSv1.2, silently installs it via msiexec /i /qn /norestart to %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Stardock Smart DeElevation Tool\, then deletes itself. DeElevate64.exe (SHA256: 22869e3326fe1de011cd500e666769027126c5c440b76837baf55139f30094e4) loads a patched DeElevator64.dll that injects a dependency on I++u.dll (the malicious loader). All seven component hashes are in the report.
- Route B delivers LegionLoader (also known as CurlyGate, RobotDropper, Satacom) through a double-nested password-protected 7z chain. The staging script downloads J8QkZUVJgV.7z from orbitflownetwork[.]lol using password iQQaQ7Yo41rbZ (hardcoded), extracts a second archive CarJqRHyOtBu3mI.7z whose password is in an extracted 20-byte text file, and ultimately produces a 882,716,672-byte PE whose .reloc section is padded with repeating 16-byte values to defeat upload limits and sandbox budgets. The meaningful code sits in the first ~2 MB prefix. AES-256-CBC with byte-reversal decrypts stage 2 shellcode, which manually maps the 475,648-byte LegionLoader PE (T1027.001, T1027.013, T1140). LegionLoader C2 is smashshape[.]com via POST to /nfront.php (registration and tasking) and /nback.php (results), with RC4/Base64-framed bodies and Chrome Local State key harvesting (T1555.003).
- Both PowerShell stagers share a common obfuscation template: integer-array reconstruction with a per-sample key, [scriptblock]::Create execution, $env:__ST for self-path tracking, and self-deletion before exit (T1027.010, T1059.001). Decimal IPv4 notation is used in Route A (1450003207 = 86.109.75[.]7). The MITRE ATT&CK techniques covered are T1204.004, T1059.001, T1105, T1027.010, T1027.001, T1027.013, T1140, T1218.007, T1574.002, T1518.001, and T1555.003.
Hunt this in three places. First, use PowerShell event 4104 to catch env:__ST, [scriptblock]::Create, and large integer arrays; flag scripts run from %TEMP% with -NoProfile -ep bypass or -w hidden containing a URL or decimal IP (8-10 digit sequence after hxxp://). Second, correlate PowerShell spawning 7zr.exe with -p and -y flags followed by execution of a randomly named binary from the extraction directory. Third, watch for module loads from %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Stardock Smart DeElevation Tool\ and compare DLL hashes against known-good Stardock inventory. For LegionLoader C2, alert on form-urlencoded POSTs to /nfront.php or /nback.php whose body is a single base64 blob. Full IOC table and hashes are in the Forescout report.

First, use PowerShell event 4104 to catch env:__ST, [scriptblock]::Create, and large integer arrays; flag scripts run from %TEMP% with -NoProfile -ep bypass or -w hidden containing a URL or decimal IP (8-10 digit sequence after hxxp://). Second, correlate PowerShell spawning 7zr.exe with -p and -y flags followed by execution of a randomly named binary from the extraction directory. Third, watch for module loads from %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Stardock Smart DeElevation Tool\ and compare DLL hashes against known-good Stardock inventory. For LegionLoader C2, alert on form-urlencoded POSTs to /nfront.php or /nback.php whose body is a single base64 blob. Full IOC table and hashes are in the Forescout report.

item.title: More Critical Bugs in Adobe Experience Manager: Pre-Auth RCE
item.description:
Pre-auth RCE chain on Adobe Experience Manager Cloud: unauthenticated file read via XXE in CreateCoralTreeServlet chains to IMS credential theft and Groovy script execution on the author instance. Fully patched on Cloud; on-prem instances need urgent upgrade.
The attack chain, step by step:
- Dispatcher bypass unlocks BulkImportConfigServlet without credentials. The dispatcher's POST filter rule (/0014) matches on the full URL, so a request to /content/x.bulkimportConfig.json/import00.importJob.json.bulkimportConfig.form.html passes through. AEM's Sling URL parser then strips the suffix and routes the request to the servlet, letting an unauthenticated attacker create a JCR configuration node that kicks off an S3-to-Azure blob import. The GET to trigger the job uses the existing dispatcher bypass: /conf/global/settings/dam/import/import00.importJob.json;x='.css/'?operation=RUN slips through the extension whitelist rule (/0011).
- Arbitrary file upload into /content/dam/collections/public gives the attacker a writable, world-readable JCR path. Because createrendition service principals hold write access there and the everyone principal holds jcr:read, any content imported lands in a location accessible anonymously. Content-Disposition: attachment initially blocks XSS, but DownloadServlet's inline selector check is performed outside normal Sling routing, so appending .inline.coredownload to the resource path flips the header to inline and makes persistent XSS viable.
- CreateCoralTreeServlet exposes an in-band XXE. The servlet delegates XML Schema parsing to xmlschema-core-2.2.3's XmlSchemaCollection, which constructs a DocumentBuilder with DTD processing and external entity resolution enabled and no mitigating features set on the DocumentBuilderFactory. A crafted .xsd imported via the bulk import primitive, then requested as /content/dam/collections/public/import00.xsd.schematree.json;x='.css/', returns file contents embedded in the JSON response. Java's directory listing behavior also makes recursive filesystem enumeration trivial.
- XXE on the Cloud pod yields IMS service account credentials. The /var/run/s6/container_environment directory and /mnt/ims-yaml-file/rt-service-user.yaml expose a JWT-based technical account (clientId, clientSecret, privateKey, orgId) with ent_aem_cloud_sdk and ent_cloudmgr_sdk metascopes. Those credentials authenticate to ims-na1.adobelogin[.]com and return a bearer token, giving full access to the associated AEM Cloud author instance.
- Author access completes the chain via /bin/asynccommand. AsyncOperationServlet's BULK_OPERATION copies a script parameter onto an async job; GroovyScriptRunner compiles and executes it. The report demonstrated OS command execution (id, ping to an out-of-band callback) and exfiltration by writing command output to /content/dam/collections/public/output.json and reading it back over HTTP, requiring no external listener infrastructure.
DFIR takeaway: If you run AEM Cloud, Adobe has patched this chain; confirm your version is current. For on-prem, treat the individual vulnerabilities as critical standalone issues. In a suspected compromise, look for anonymous POST requests hitting paths matching *.bulkimportConfig.form.html in dispatcher and Jetty access logs, GET requests to /conf/global/settings/dam/import/ with path parameter segments like ;x='.css/', unexpected nodes created under /content/dam/collections/public in the JCR, requests to *.schematree.json with outbound DNS or HTTP initiated by the AEM process, and any POST to /bin/asynccommand followed by reads of output nodes. IMS credential files at /mnt/ims-yaml-file/ and environment variable dumps at /var/run/s6/container_environment should be treated as fully compromised if XXE was reachable. The full technical detail, including request structures and servlet code, is in the Searchlight Labs report.

item.title: The GhostX Ecosystem: Forged in Transit, Licensed to Deceive
item.description:
GhostBat RAT evolves into a full MaaS ecosystem targeting Indian 🇮🇳 Android users, introducing transparent PIN-intercept overlays over legitimate Google Pay and MobiKwik apps across 60 financial platforms.
Key findings:
- The GhostX ecosystem is not a single malware family. Cyble's investigation into fake mParivahan and eChallan APKs exposed a structured Firebase backend (project identifier: ghostx-panel) containing admin, user, bot-user, and device-management records with role fields, session tokens, and login fingerprints. Active changes to SMS lure content, phishing URLs, vehicle registration numbers, and recipient phone numbers confirmed live operator management, and the architecture suggests a potential Malware-as-a-Service model with distinct operator tiers.
- The Ghost Overlay technique (T1453, T1516) is the most operationally significant new capability. Instead of overlaying a fake login page, GhostBat RAT places a transparent 12-region keypad grid (TYPE_ACCESSIBILITY_OVERLAY) over the real Google Pay and MobiKwik PIN-entry screens, intercepts each tap, maps coordinates to digits, and uses AccessibilityService.dispatchGesture() to replay the same touch into the legitimate app so the transaction completes normally. The victim never sees a fake interface. Captured digits are buffered and exfiltrated to hxxps://api.cloudsettle[.]org/pin-data with source metadata tagged ghost_overlay. A broader accessibility keylogger (T1417.001) extends the same PIN-capture logic to 60 Android financial packages including PhonePe, Paytm, BHIM, SBI UPI, CRED, BharatPe, and others, handled by a dedicated PinUploadWorker posting to /pin-data.
- The loader chain has diversified across at least six implementations (T1406.002): AES-CBC native loaders, XOR/SPKZ/SPK1 containers, Java in-memory DEX loaders, a remote-downloader variant that validates a SHA-256 hash before installing a second-stage APK (T1407), and now a libnetbridge[.]so native loader that processes the encrypted asset assets/isti52q4 through an RC4-like pass, then AES-256-GCM, then zlib decompression into an MSZ1/MSP1 container, recovering a split-APK (base.apk plus split_config.dex.apk). Hash- and outer-APK-based detections will not provide durable coverage across loader generations.
- C2 infrastructure is dynamically managed through Firebase Remote Config (Firebase project: andromeda-d389d). The base_url parameter lets operators swap the active REST backend without touching or redistributing the APK, so api.cloudsettle[.]org is the observed default, not a fixed indicator. Operator-controlled flags ghost_overlay_enabled and ghost_overlay_packages govern overlay activation per device. The backend exposes 14 documented REST endpoints covering SMS batch upload, call-log collection, SIM info, FCM token registration, PIN data, live keylog status, and call-forwarding state, alongside a configurable WebSocket channel. Distribution runs through smishing links to phishing pages mimicking Parivahan or a fake Google Play store, with GitHub repositories also actively used to host malicious APKs (T1660, T1655.001).
Practitioner takeaway: on Android forensics, prioritize Accessibility Service grant records, the list of packages in pin_target_packages and ghost_overlay_packages retrieved from Firebase, and network artifacts showing POST requests to /pin-data and the 13 other documented C2 endpoints under api.cloudsettle[.]org. For hunting across enterprise mobile fleets, flag any APK requesting Accessibility Service that also holds a native library named libnetbridge[.]so or an asset matching the isti52q4 naming pattern. IOCs and the full 60-package targeted application list are in the Cyble report.

item.title: [0day-rubbish] SmartBear Collaborator Server 15.1.15101 authenticated DOORS/Simulink review-file upload zip-slip to anonymous webroot Groovy Server Page execution as uid 1001 (7.5)
item.description:
SmartBear Collaborator Server 15.1.15101 carries a zip-slip path traversal that lets one low-privilege account plant a Groovy Server Page in the Tomcat webroot, then any anonymous client executes it with a plain GET. CVSS 3.1 score: 7.5 (AC:H); conditional 8.8 where the upload tree is service-owned.
Key findings:
- The root cause is CWE-22 in two code instances. ReviewService.addDoorsFiles dispatches to DoorsFilesUploadService.upload, which builds the extraction destination at line 78 using File(uploadContext.getDestVersionDir(), fileName) with no normalize(), no canonical-path containment test, and no extension filter. An entry named ../../../../../webapps/ROOT/payload.gsp escapes the per-review version directory and lands in the Tomcat webroot. The sibling SimulinkFilesUploadService.copyFilesFromZip at line 188 shares the identical defect via destDir.resolve(zipEntry.getName()).toFile() with no startsWith check, reachable from ReviewService.addSimulinkFiles. The depth is deterministic: depth = 4 + n, where n is the number of path segments in the zip base name.
- Execution is first-party configuration, not a second bug. ROOT/web.xml lines 271-278 map *.gsp to groovy.servlet.TemplateServlet on the unauthenticated surface. A plain anonymous GET of the planted path compiles and evaluates it in memory. The confirmed identity string was uid=1001(collab) gid=1001(collab) groups=1001(collab) with an empty capability set. The write requires one low-privilege authenticated account (PR:L, not PR:H); administrator status is neither needed nor sufficient, as the system administrator account is refused by addDoorsFiles unless getAllowSysadminReviews() is true.
- Exploitability is deployment-shape dependent, and the researchers are explicit about it. The official container image used exactly as shipped blocks the chain: the webserver directory is declared as a VOLUME but never created by the installer, so the container runtime creates the mount point as drwxr-xr-x owned by root, and the first Files.createDirectories call at HtmlBaseFilesUploadService[.]java:77 fails with EACCES before any archive entry is written. The 7.5 headline reflects AC:H for this condition. The conditional 8.8 (AC:L) applies to native installs and any container deployment where that directory is service-owned, a shape the researchers inferred from the installer archive rather than observed on a live native host.
- The blast radius at uid=1001 covers the entire installation. The HSQLDB file hsqldb/database.data stores password digests as unsalted ASCII MD5. The JNDI datasource at conf/Catalina/localhost/ROOT.xml uses username="sa" with an empty password. Source-control passwords and OAuth client secrets are encrypted under a constant key embedded in EncryptUtils[.]java:31-32, readable by the service account. A separate unauthenticated double-decoded traversal in WebserverServlet[.]java:208 (new File(root, URLDecoder.decode(pathInfo)) with no canonicalization) provides a second independent read primitive requiring no account at all; it is a distinct finding and not folded into the 7.5 score.
- Detection is harder than response codes suggest. HTTP 200 accompanies the blocked shape, the partially-failed shape, and successful exploitation alike. The product audit log records only a review creation and a file-addition line naming a directory under /webserver/doors/, never the entry name or traversal. Groovy compiles in memory, leaving zero compiled output in the Tomcat work directory. What does persist is the .gsp file itself: the shipped installation contains exactly one Groovy template at ROOT/jsp/views/json_tester.gsp, so any additional .gsp under webapps/ROOT is anomalous. The triggering anonymous GET carries no session and receives X-Smart-Bear-Not-Logged-In: true.
Practitioner takeaway: Until a vendor patch exists, answer your own exposure question by checking the ownership of the collaborator-webserver directory relative to the Tomcat working directory (/usr/local/ccollab_server/tomcat/collaborator-webserver by default). If it is root-owned while the service runs as uid 1001, the container shape blocks the chain at the filesystem; if it is service-owned, treat the instance as exposed. Place file-integrity monitoring on webapps/ROOT alerting on any new file and on any .gsp other than json_tester.gsp. Hunt for the two-request shape: a multipart POST to /services/json/v1 whose json part names ReviewService.addDoorsFiles, followed by an anonymous GET for a .gsp path not present in the shipped installation. On any instance where compromise is suspected, rotate all stored credentials: source-control tokens, OAuth secrets, directory-service bind credentials, and all Collaborator account passwords, because all are readable or decryptable at uid=1001. The report and a Python 3 proof-of-concept are published at 0day-rubbish[.]com/blog/smartbear-collaborator-doors-upload-zip-slip-webroot-gsp-rce. No CVE has been assigned yet.

item.title: [0day-rubbish] Dataedo Portal 26.2.8 with Dataedo Agent 26.2.8 unrestricted scheduler job-type deserialization to Agent-host command execution (8.1)
item.description:
Dataedo Portal 26.2.8 has a static AES key baked into its shipped DLL that exposes repo credentials, chaining into unrestricted Hangfire deserialization on the Agent host for OS command execution, scored CVSS 8.1 High with no patch and no CVE yet assigned.
Key findings:
- The chain starts at GET /api/repository/connection-string, which returns the repository DB credential encrypted with SimpleAES: AES-256-CBC with a 32-byte key and 16-byte IV hardcoded as byte-array literals in the shipped Dataedo.Settings.dll, byte-identical across every build and referenced from 19 assemblies. The same static pair is published in the proof-of-concept. In the tested deployment the recovered login was sa, a sysadmin-level principal over the database that also holds the Hangfire scheduler storage in the [Scheduler] schema. No gadget chain is required: the invocation document names System.Diagnostics.Process/Start directly, with cmd.exe and the payload as arguments, inserted as two rows into [Scheduler].Job and [Scheduler].JobQueue.
- The Agent side registers no ITypeResolver restriction and no invocation allowlist with either its default or priority Hangfire queue. FilterInitializer calls GlobalJobFilters.Clear() and adds four filters, none of which constrains execution type at runtime: the two IClientFilter implementations return early unless the type implements ISchedulerTaskExecutor, the IApplyStateFilter reacts only to DeletedState transitions, and AutomaticRetry is set to Attempts=0. After Clear() nothing in the execution path inspects the invocation type, declaring type, method name, or arguments. Execution was observed at nt authority\system when the Agent ran as a SYSTEM-privileged service, and at the local administrator account when launched interactively. The report is explicit that the SYSTEM outcome reflects the test harness service configuration, not a confirmed universal default.
- Exploitation requires PR:H (role action 11 or above on the Portal), a network path to the repository listener, and at least one Agent attached to that repository. The CVSS 3.1 vector is AV:N/AC:H/PR:H/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H = 8.1. Scope is Changed because the impacted component is a separately installed process on a separate host reached only through the repository database. A conditional vector of 9.1 applies where an attached Agent and reachable listener are known, which is the ordinary topology for any deployment using scheduling features.
- The adjacent disclosure group (unscored, no patch) adds: 18 ungated routes on RepositoryController enabling anonymous repository registration during any unconfigured window; anonymous rewrite of configuration[WEB_CATALOG_URL] via POST /api/repository/connect-and-upgrade on a healthy instance, converting the portal into a credential-phishing surface; outbound TDS to attacker-named hosts through available-databases (NetNTLMv2 exposure on Windows); SSRF through /api/text-editor/link reaching internal services and cloud instance metadata (HTTP 200 observed); wildcard CORS (SetIsOriginAllowed(_ => true) with AllowCredentials and SameSite=None) covering the entire cookie-authenticated /api/* surface; and a default JWT signing key (shipped GUID, ValidateIssuer=false, ValidateAudience=false) affecting container and non-wizard deployments.
- Detection signals the report names: an InvocationData value in [Scheduler].Job whose Type field names anything outside the vendor's scheduler job namespace, especially System.Diagnostics.Process; a State.Result of "Can not serialize the return value" on a completed job; PerformanceDuration in the low single-digit milliseconds for a non-vendor job type; shell binaries in the Arguments column; a JobQueue row whose FetchedAt is never populated (preparation with no consumer); unexpected child processes of the Agent service on the Agent host; and POST traffic to repository registration and connect-and-upgrade routes from unauthenticated clients, or a change in configuration[WEB_CATALOG_URL] or appsettings.json.
Practitioner takeaway: No patch exists and no CVE has been assigned. Until one arrives, restrict network access to the repository listener to Portal and Agent hosts only, enable database auditing on [Scheduler].Job and [Scheduler].JobQueue inserts and alert on the Type and State.Result signals above, treat any principal with [Scheduler] write access as holding command execution on every attached Agent host, complete first-run repository configuration immediately after install, rotate the repository credential and treat every prior copy as exposed (any repo-management principal can recover it on demand), inventory Dataedo-Web-backup-*.zip artifacts as credential material, strip reflected Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with credentials at the reverse proxy, and rotate the JWT signing key on any deployment that did not pass through the installer's API-configuration wizard. Treat the Agent host as a crown-jewel system for the duration.

In the tested deployment the recovered login was sa, a sysadmin-level principal over the database that also holds the Hangfire scheduler storage in the [Scheduler] schema. No gadget chain is required: the invocation document names System.Diagnostics.Process/Start directly, with cmd.exe and the payload as arguments, inserted as two rows into [Scheduler].Job and [Scheduler].JobQueue.

- The Agent side registers no ITypeResolver restriction and no invocation allowlist with either its default or priority Hangfire queue. FilterInitializer calls GlobalJobFilters.Clear() and adds four filters, none of which constrains execution type at runtime: the two IClientFilter implementations return early unless the type implements ISchedulerTaskExecutor, the IApplyStateFilter reacts only to DeletedState transitions, and AutomaticRetry is set to Attempts=0. After Clear() nothing in the execution path inspects the invocation type, declaring type, method name, or arguments. Execution was observed at nt authority\system when the Agent ran as a SYSTEM-privileged service, and at the local administrator account when launched interactively. The report is explicit that the SYSTEM outcome reflects the test harness service configuration, not a confirmed universal default.

- Exploitation requires PR:H (role action 11 or above on the Portal), a network path to the repository listener, and at least one Agent attached to that repository. The CVSS 3.1 vector is AV:N/AC:H/PR:H/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H = 8.1. Scope is Changed because the impacted component is a separately installed process on a separate host reached only through the repository database. A conditional vector of 9.1 applies where an attached Agent and reachable listener are known, which is the ordinary topology for any deployment using scheduling features.

- The adjacent disclosure group (unscored, no patch) adds: 18 ungated routes on RepositoryController enabling anonymous repository registration during any unconfigured window; anonymous rewrite of configuration[WEB_CATALOG_URL] via POST /api/repository/connect-and-upgrade on a healthy instance, converting the portal into a credential-phishing surface; outbound TDS to attacker-named hosts through available-databases (NetNTLMv2 exposure on Windows); SSRF through /api/text-editor/link reaching internal services and cloud instance metadata (HTTP 200 observed); wildcard CORS (SetIsOriginAllowed(_ => true) with AllowCredentials and SameSite=None) covering the entire cookie-authenticated /api/* surface; and a default JWT signing key (shipped GUID, ValidateIssuer=false, ValidateAudience=false) affecting container and non-wizard deployments.

- Detection signals the report names: an InvocationData value in [Scheduler].Job whose Type field names anything outside the vendor's scheduler job namespace, especially System.Diagnostics.Process; a State.Result of "Can not serialize the return value" on a completed job; PerformanceDuration in the low single-digit milliseconds for a non-vendor job type; shell binaries in the Arguments column; a JobQueue row whose FetchedAt is never populated (preparation with no consumer); unexpected child processes of the Agent service on the Agent host; and POST traffic to repository registration and connect-and-upgrade routes from unauthenticated clients, or a change in configuration[WEB_CATALOG_URL] or appsettings.json.

Practitioner takeaway: No patch exists and no CVE has been assigned. Until one arrives, restrict network access to the repository listener to Portal and Agent hosts only, enable database auditing on [Scheduler].Job and [Scheduler].JobQueue inserts and alert on the Type and State.Result signals above, treat any principal with [Scheduler] write access as holding command execution on every attached Agent host, complete first-run repository configuration immediately after install, rotate the repository credential and treat every prior copy as exposed (any repo-management principal can recover it on demand), inventory Dataedo-Web-backup-*.zip artifacts as credential material, strip reflected Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with credentials at the reverse proxy, and rotate the JWT signing key on any deployment that did not pass through the installer's API-configuration wizard. Treat the Agent host as a crown-jewel system for the duration.

item.title: The Threat of AI-Driven Autonomous Penetration Testing, as Examined by ARTEX
item.description:
AI-driven autonomous penetration testing is no longer theoretical. AhnLab ASEC tracked an internet-exposed ARTEX instance and found operational attack artifacts on associated hosts, confirming the tool is being used beyond proof-of-concept.
- AhnLab identified 600 public IPs hosting ARTEX instances, with 90.2% concentrated across the US 🇺🇸, China 🇨🇳, Hong Kong, and Singapore 🇸🇬. As of October 14, 2026, approximately 900 IPs associated with the ARTEX operating system were publicly accessible. Two of those 600 IPs were directly tied to operational attack directories, and investigators recovered 51 files across those two open directories, including ws[.]sh (a script written to send commands to an ASPX web shell), pivot_relay.ps1 (configured to relay external connections to internal RDP), extract_hprof.py (written to extract credentials from JVM heap dumps), P.class (designed to download and execute a Linux implant), and LocaleMgr.exe (containing strings indicating command execution, file manipulation, and tunneling). Scan results in the second directory listed 85 active systems in a Kubernetes Pod network and 8 in a separate internal network. The IOC table in the report contains 2 IPs (134.122.137[.]132 and 204.194.51[.]54) and 18 MD5 hashes tied to these directories.
- ARTEX operates through three agent roles: Goals (organizes objectives and test scope), Planner (reviews gathered information and determines next steps), and Worker (executes tools and records verified results). Asset context is stored in a PostgreSQL-backed Asset Graph and Exploration Graph, allowing the system to reason across tasks without repeating prior reconnaissance. On the target side, logs record the tool requests and process behavior, not any agent name, which limits visibility into the AI layer driving the attack.
- In two controlled reproduction tests, ARTEX received only a brief plaintext objective with no vulnerability details, no tool guidance, and no human intervention mid-run. Against a web server with a file upload vulnerability, it located the upload path, deployed a web shell, and executed a program on a Windows 11 host. Against an Apache ActiveMQ 5.15.15 instance, it autonomously identified CVE-2023-46604 on TCP port 61616, modified XML to establish a PowerShell shell, and then pivoted to achieve remote command execution on four internal hosts following initial access to the boundary server BEACHHEAD01. External tools including nmap, nxc, and Impacket were selected and invoked without user instruction.
- User-Agent detection is unreliable as a primary control. ARTEX recorded "artex-selfupdate" for GitHub update checks, "norma/0.4" for web page access, and "curl/VERSION" for file uploads during testing. The source code specifies "artex-enrich/1.0" and "Mozilla/5.0 (Spa-api-recon)" variants exist but were not active in the analyzed version. Non-HTTP communications (SMB, OpenWire on port 61616, RDP relay) leave no User-Agent trace at all, and threat actors can trivially modify or suppress these values.
DFIR takeaway: Do not anchor your hunt to User-Agent strings. The real signal is behavioral sequencing across log sources. Look for the chain: external service scan or probe, followed by file write or web shell creation on a web-accessible path, followed by a new process spawned from a web server process, followed by outbound SMB or RDP from that host to internal segments. Correlate web access logs, firewall connection logs, and endpoint process execution logs together. For the ActiveMQ angle specifically, the report ties exploitation of CVE-2023-46604 to TCP port 61616 and XML modification as the mechanism for shell establishment, so watch for unexpected child processes under ActiveMQ service processes and PowerShell spawning in that context. The full IOC table with 2 IPs and 18 MD5 hashes is in the report.

item.title: AI-Found Linux Kernel Flaw Gives Local Users Root, and Can Break a Guest Out to the Host
item.description:
CVE-2026-74580 "Vghost": a Linux kernel vhost flaw gives any local user reliable kernel read/write and root across nearly a decade of kernels, with a second path that lets a VM escape to the host's QEMU process.
Key findings:
- The bug lives in Linux's vhost subsystem, reachable by opening /dev/vhost-net or /dev/vhost-vsock. A stale translation cache, introduced across two separate commits (a 2017 cache addition in Linux 4.11 and a 2020 check relocation in Linux 5.9), lets VHOST_SET_VRING_ADDR and VHOST_SET_VRING_NUM reconfigure a live ring's addresses without invalidating that cache. Subsequent copies use the old, unchecked mapping, producing an out-of-bounds kernel read and write. The local-privilege-escalation chain is deterministic, needs no heap grooming and no timing luck, bypasses KASLR, and reaches root. No public exploitation has been observed.
- The guest-to-host escape is narrower but severe. It requires a virtio device behind a virtual IOMMU with iommu_platform enabled and vhost running in device-IOTLB mode. An untrusted guest triggers the same stale-cache path, causing the host kernel to write out of bounds into the host's QEMU process. From there, an attacker can overwrite a function pointer in QEMU and redirect host execution, or crash the hypervisor. The kernel[.]org CVE team scores this 8.8 with scope marked "changed" because the write crosses the guest-to-host boundary. Red Hat scores it 7.3, Amazon 7.8, Oracle 7.3.
- Affected range is Linux 4.11 through 7.2-rc4. Tencent confirmed the full local-to-root chain on Ubuntu 26.04, RHEL 9.8, Amazon Linux 2023, Microsoft Azure Linux 3.0, and Oracle Linux 10.2. On Ubuntu, the device node is group-restricted to kvm, so the entry point is a kvm group member. On the other four images, /dev/vhost-net and /dev/vhost-vsock were world-readable at mode 0666, meaning any local user was in scope. The fix is commit de845981da67, which clears the cache on every ring reconfiguration. First fixed stable versions range from 5.10.265 through 7.1.9 across seven maintained branches. Red Hat, Amazon, and Oracle have shipped fixes; Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04 fixes were still in progress as of October 13.
- The flaw was found with help from Corvus AI, a multi-agent kernel vulnerability research pipeline Tencent Zhuque Lab built in-house. The upstream commit credits it with an Assisted-by line. This is the same team and toolchain that disclosed an 18-year-old SCTP kernel flaw in August 2026, also reaching root and container escape. This is machine-assisted research, not an autonomous attack.
Practitioner takeaway: check your vhost device node permissions before a patch lands. Run "stat /dev/vhost-net /dev/vhost-vsock" on every Linux host and container host in your environment. If either shows mode 0666, remove world access and restrict the owning group to trusted virtualization services immediately. Treat kvm or equivalent group membership as a sensitive privilege while the vulnerable kernel runs. For the guest-to-host path, no workaround exists: the patched kernel is the only remedy, so prioritize hypervisor hosts, cloud-adjacent Linux images, and any multi-tenant environment where local access is broadly granted. The report includes working proof-of-concept demos for both attack chains.

item.title: Frostbitten in France: A Danfoss StoreView Internet Exposure Report
item.description:
Attackers hit hundreds of French 🇫🇷 supermarkets on October 11, pushing Danfoss AK-SM 800A refrigeration controllers into defrost mode, spoiling food and causing fires. Three chained CVEs in internet-exposed management interfaces were the enabling conditions.
- The vulnerability chain starts with CVE-2025-41450 (disclosed March 2025, fixed in firmware 4.2), which let an unauthenticated actor compute a valid admin password from the current calendar date with no credentials. CVE-2025-41451 and CVE-2025-41452 (disclosed August 2025, fixed in 4.3.1) added authenticated command execution and interface disruption. In August 2026, Claroty demonstrated chaining CVE-2025-41450 with CVE-2025-41451 to reach remote code execution. That proof-of-concept preceded this attack by roughly two months.
- Censys identified 1,825 StoreView hosts in France 🇫🇷 on October 11. Of those, 1,158 ran firmware below 4.2, meaning the date-derived admin password was still valid. By October 14, that count had dropped to 537, a 71% fall. The key finding: patched and unpatched hosts disappeared at the same rate (roughly 70% each), meaning operators pulled devices off the internet rather than patching. The worldwide picture is worse: the three largest globally exposed version groups are 3.3.0 (560 hosts), 4.3.1 (511), and 3.2.6 (437). Ten of the twelve most-exposed countries have more than 60% of their hosts below 4.3.1, led by Poland 🇵🇱 at 81% and Romania 🇷🇴 at 80%.
- The Censys report details a fingerprinting method that responders can replicate: the login-page version string does not match the actual firmware. The real version maps to the Last-Modified HTTP header of html/index.html inside the firmware package. The report extracted timestamps from all 18 public .spk update files available at sm800a.danfoss[.]com/sw_shared/, correlating each to a UTC build date, and matched those dates to Censys scan data. The SHA-256 of the 4.3.1 update is 5a19ee33d9d9fa26302bbf2b1875475c9e97979528fd382e87de39a645b96af2.
- CERT-FR issued emergency alert CERTFR-2026-ALE-012 calling for immediate internet disconnection. The incident echoes a confirmed August 2026 event where US 🇺🇸 Department of Defense commissary freezers went into defrost mode, though no vendor or CVE was ever confirmed for that incident. The pattern is consistent: internet-exposed OT with no network segmentation, running end-of-life firmware that cannot be patched because replacement is cost-prohibitive.
For responders and OT defenders: use the Censys query "host[.]services.endpoints.http.html_title = 'Danfoss StoreView'" to find exposed instances in your environment or on your client's ASM scope. Check the HTTP Last-Modified header against the build date table in the report to determine true firmware version, not the login-page string. If the build date predates July 31, 2025 (the 4.3.1 build timestamp), the device is vulnerable to at least CVE-2025-41451 and CVE-2025-41452; predating March 4, 2025 means all three CVEs are open. The right remediation is network isolation, not patching alone.

item.title: Determined Attacker Uploads Malicious Webshells to Parks and Rec Management Platform Servers
item.description:
A determined attacker hit multiple tenants of a recreation management platform across four acts, registering member accounts to upload .aspx webshells, hunting cardholder data, and ultimately trojanizing a jQuery file to harvest credentials from every visitor to the login page.
Key findings:
- Initial access came not from the six hours of failed brute-forcing, IIS 8.3 tilde enumeration, WebDAV method abuse, or upload-handler parser bypasses, but from simply registering a legitimate member account and abusing the upload function to drop .aspx webshells into /documents/MemberFiles/. Fourteen files were uploaded on Server 1, using the platform's own naming convention (accountID_memberID_UUID.aspx). The webshell keys wf9x (Act 1) and m7Qx2pL9 (Acts 2-4) identify which shell was in use. The attacker's user-agent Mozilla/5.0+(Windows+NT;+Windows+NT+10.0;+zh-CN)+WindowsPowerShell/5.1.22621.1037 places the locale as Simplified Chinese 🇨🇳.
- Post-access enumeration was systematic and payment-focused. After running whoami, hostname, ipconfig, netstat, and appcmd.exe to map the IIS environment, the attacker parsed web.config files as XML via PowerShell to extract SQL credentials, then used sqlcmd to connect directly to the database hunting for cardholder data. They also ran findstr across Fortis webhook log files at E:\Content\info_fortis\Webhooks\ looking for exp_date, cvv, card_number, first_six, and last_four fields, and searched for AuthorizeNet, Fortis, CardConnect, BluePay, and Stripe references across the content directory.
- The attacker adapted across all three servers, getting quieter each time. On Server 3 they copied webshells disguised as css_bundle.aspx, jquery.validate.min.aspx, and webresource.aspx into IIS include and virtual directory paths, then timestomped those files by inheriting timestamps from E:\Websites\REDACTED[.]com\http\web.config, making them blend into the legitimate file timeline. When defenders cleaned but did not fully lock the third server, the attacker returned using the same registered account and escalated to supply-chain-style payload injection.
- Act 4 was the most damaging attempt. The attacker dropped Base64-encoded files into C:\Windows\Temp (plant_ccrtc_mousewheel.ps1.b64, plant_ccrtc_fast.ps1.b64, ccrtc_sdk_init.js.b64), decoded them to .ps1 and .js, then used the PS1 scripts to locate and append an obfuscated payload into the legitimate jQuery asset jquery.mousewheel-3.0.6.pack.js loaded by /auth/default.aspx. The injected JavaScript pulled a second-stage payload from hxxps://chat.ririmochii.workers[.]dev/core[.]js and established WebRTC and WebSocket C2 channels to hxxps://fk.bubuneeko.workers[.]dev/_cf/rel, hxxps://fk.bubuneeko.workers[.]dev/_cf/ice, and wss://fk.bubuneeko.workers[.]dev/_cf/soc to harvest credentials from every visiting browser in real time. An idempotency guard (function _0x9d66) prevented duplicate payload writes. The PS1 scripts contain comments consistent with AI-generated code, including literal instruction fragments such as "Fast plant: candidate paths only, no drive recurse."
Takeaway: On any IIS-hosted multi-tenant platform, start your hunt in the member file upload directories. Look for .aspx files matching a member account naming pattern in paths like /documents/MemberFiles/. Pull IIS logs and cross-reference w3wp.exe spawning cmd.exe or powershell.exe as a child process. Check C:\Windows\Temp for .b64 files decoded to .ps1 or .js. Audit jQuery and other shared JS assets for appended content and compare file hashes against known-good versions. Examine file timestamps for outliers where creation, modified, and accessed times are identical to nearby legitimate files, a strong indicator of timestomping. The full IOC table, including six SHA256 hashes and the C2 domains, is in the Huntress report.
