item.title: CVE-2026-74580: Linux vhost stale IOTLB cache leading to LPE and VM escape
item.description:
CVE-2026-74580 (CVSS 8.8) is a stale IOTLB metadata cache bug in Linux vhost frontends with a working local-to-root exploit and a confirmed VM escape path. Actively reproduced on Ubuntu, RHEL, Amazon Linux, Azure Linux, and Oracle Linux. Patch now.
Key details:
- The root cause sits in vq->meta_iotlb[], the cache that stores IOTLB mappings for descriptor, available, and used rings. VHOST_SET_VRING_ADDR and VHOST_SET_VRING_NUM replace the vring configuration without flushing that cache. A subsequent cache hit skips range validation and computes a translated pointer as "old_map->addr + new_addr - old_map->start", which then feeds directly into raw_copy_to_user() or raw_copy_from_user() with no bounds check. The defect traces to the interaction of two upstream commits: f88949138058 (metadata cache introduction) and 0210a8db2aec (deferred GIOVA validation).
- The local privilege escalation chain is fully demonstrated: a uid=1000 user primes meta_iotlb[], issues VHOST_SET_VRING_ADDR to swap the address while the stale cache survives, repoints the descriptor ring to leak 8 bytes via an IOTLB_MISS response, reads IDT[0] to recover the KASLR slide, then repoints the used ring to overwrite modprobe_path at runtime. Triggering request_module() executes a memfd payload as uid=0. The chain was reproduced with one generic x86-64 exploit across all five tested distributions. A public PoC is on GitHub.
- The VM escape path requires a guest configured with vIOMMU, iommu_platform, and VIRTIO_F_RING_RESET. The guest primes the used-ring metadata cache, issues a queue reset followed by a new queue address via VHOST_SET_VRING_ADDR, and re-enables the queue. The stale cache survives the reset, and the resulting used-ring write escapes guest RAM into the QEMU heap, corrupting QOM object tables and yielding controlled QEMU RIP.
- Exposure is worse than expected on default installs. Ubuntu 26.04 exposes /dev/vhost-vsock as 0660 root:kvm (kvm group membership required), but RHEL 9.8, Amazon Linux 2023, Azure Linux 3.0, and Oracle Linux 10.2 all expose it as 0666, meaning any local user on those systems can reach the exploit without any group membership. Affected device nodes include /dev/vhost-net, /dev/vhost-vsock, /dev/vhost-scsi, and /dev/vhost-vdpa-*.
- The upstream fix resets the vring metadata cache inside vhost_vring_set_num_addr(), forcing reconfigured addresses back through IOTLB validation. On unpatched virtualization hosts, treat any QEMU crash with heap corruption signals as a potential exploitation attempt against this path. Check /dev/vhost-* permissions immediately with "ls -la /dev/vhost-*": world-readable (0666) nodes on RHEL, Amazon Linux, Azure Linux, or Oracle Linux systems mean the local chain is reachable by any user. item.content:encoded:
CVE-2026-74580 (CVSS 8.8) is a stale IOTLB metadata cache bug in Linux vhost frontends with a working local-to-root exploit and a confirmed VM escape path. Actively reproduced on Ubuntu, RHEL, Amazon Linux, Azure Linux, and Oracle Linux. Patch now.

Key details:

- The root cause sits in vq->meta_iotlb[], the cache that stores IOTLB mappings for descriptor, available, and used rings. VHOST_SET_VRING_ADDR and VHOST_SET_VRING_NUM replace the vring configuration without flushing that cache. A subsequent cache hit skips range validation and computes a translated pointer as "old_map->addr + new_addr - old_map->start", which then feeds directly into raw_copy_to_user() or raw_copy_from_user() with no bounds check. The defect traces to the interaction of two upstream commits: f88949138058 (metadata cache introduction) and 0210a8db2aec (deferred GIOVA validation).

- The local privilege escalation chain is fully demonstrated: a uid=1000 user primes meta_iotlb[], issues VHOST_SET_VRING_ADDR to swap the address while the stale cache survives, repoints the descriptor ring to leak 8 bytes via an IOTLB_MISS response, reads IDT[0] to recover the KASLR slide, then repoints the used ring to overwrite modprobe_path at runtime. Triggering request_module() executes a memfd payload as uid=0. The chain was reproduced with one generic x86-64 exploit across all five tested distributions. A public PoC is on GitHub.

- The VM escape path requires a guest configured with vIOMMU, iommu_platform, and VIRTIO_F_RING_RESET. The guest primes the used-ring metadata cache, issues a queue reset followed by a new queue address via VHOST_SET_VRING_ADDR, and re-enables the queue. The stale cache survives the reset, and the resulting used-ring write escapes guest RAM into the QEMU heap, corrupting QOM object tables and yielding controlled QEMU RIP.

- Exposure is worse than expected on default installs. Ubuntu 26.04 exposes /dev/vhost-vsock as 0660 root:kvm (kvm group membership required), but RHEL 9.8, Amazon Linux 2023, Azure Linux 3.0, and Oracle Linux 10.2 all expose it as 0666, meaning any local user on those systems can reach the exploit without any group membership. Affected device nodes include /dev/vhost-net, /dev/vhost-vsock, /dev/vhost-scsi, and /dev/vhost-vdpa-*.

- The upstream fix resets the vring metadata cache inside vhost_vring_set_num_addr(), forcing reconfigured addresses back through IOTLB validation. Fixed in kernel stable releases 5.10.265, 5.15.216, 6.1.183, 6.6.152, 6.12.104, 6.18.45, 7.1.9, and 7.2. Vendor advisories are live for Amazon Linux and Oracle Linux.

DFIR takeaway: For incident response, look for unexpected privilege escalation to root on Linux hypervisor or container hosts alongside unusual modprobe_path modification, which would appear as a write to the string at the kernel symbol modprobe_path (default /sbin/modprobe) followed by a short-lived root process and a restoration write. On unpatched virtualization hosts, treat any QEMU crash with heap corruption signals as a potential exploitation attempt against this path. Check /dev/vhost-* permissions immediately with "ls -la /dev/vhost-*": world-readable (0666) nodes on RHEL, Amazon Linux, Azure Linux, or Oracle Linux systems mean the local chain is reachable by any user. Until patched, restrict those device nodes with chmod, prevent untrusted containers from accessing them, and do not expose vhost devices with iommu_platform to untrusted guests. Note that permission changes do not revoke already-open file descriptors. The technical write-up and PoC are publicly available.

item.title: When LLM Gateways Go Wrong: Findings from LiteLLM
item.description:
Two CVEs in LiteLLM's gateway expose any authenticated user to RCE, admin takeover, and credential theft via a missing RBAC check on a single configuration endpoint, patched in v1.83.9.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-35029 is the core flaw: the POST /config/update endpoint in litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py performs only a generic auth check (user_api_key_auth) and no subsequent role verification, while the UI session token's startswith("/config") prefix match against the ui_routes allowlist lets any logged-in user, including baseline "Internal User" accounts, reach an endpoint meant for admins only. The three immediate impacts are arbitrary file read (inject UI_LOGO_PATH into environment_variables, then call GET /get_image to retrieve any file the process can read, including secrets), admin account takeover (overwrite UI_USERNAME and UI_PASSWORD environment variables so the /login flow authenticates the attacker as PROXY_ADMIN), and RCE via pass-through endpoint configuration that triggers importlib exec_module() on a Python file downloaded from an attacker-controlled S3 or GCS bucket.
- CVE-2026-59823 is a separate SSRF: the /chat/completions endpoint accepts a user_config body parameter that constructs a new litellm.Router with attacker-supplied api_base values, routing LLM API calls, including any configured provider keys in default headers, to an arbitrary server. The configurable_clientside_auth_params restriction that guards the direct api_base and api_key fields does not apply to the user_config code path, so it bypasses the intended guardrail entirely.
- Two additional weaknesses tracked under GHSA-69x8-hrgq-fjj8 (marked duplicate): password hashes for all users are reachable by low-privileged accounts through the same UI token bypass, and those hashes are produced by a single unsalted iteration of a standard hash function, making offline cracking with rainbow tables or brute force practical once the hashes are extracted.
- The full attack chain from a low-privileged account to RCE requires no zero-day and no memory corruption: authenticate, POST to /config/update with a malicious pass_through_endpoints entry pointing to an attacker-owned S3 bucket, and LiteLLM downloads and executes the Python file at configuration load time. The proof of concept in the report uses os.makedirs() as the payload; a reverse shell is a one-line substitution.
Responder takeaway: if you run LiteLLM in your AI stack, treat any instance below v1.83.9 as fully compromised from the perspective of any authenticated user. Upgrade to v1.83.9 immediately. For forensic triage, review your proxy's persisted YAML configuration and database-stored general_settings for unexpected pass_through_endpoints entries with s3:// or gcs:// targets, and audit environment_variables stored in the config for anomalous UI_LOGO_PATH, UI_USERNAME, or UI_PASSWORD values. Check outbound network logs from the LiteLLM host for connections to S3/GCS endpoints or unexpected external IPs at LLM API call time, which would indicate SSRF exploitation of CVE-2026-59823. The report is from Check Point Research and contains the vulnerable and patched code paths.

item.title: CVE-2026-70111: One-Packet Windows Server DoS via DFS
item.description:
CVE-2026-70111: A single malformed DFS referral packet crashes Windows Server 2019, 2022, and 2025 with a kernel null-dereference in mup.sys. Patch shipped October 13, 2026; no active exploitation observed as of publication.
Key findings:
- The root cause sits in mup.sys. An earlier null-pointer guard (checking that wzExpandedName length is greater than zero before calling wcslen()) was removed from Server builds while Windows 10 retained it. A crafted DFS_REFERRAL_V3 NameList referral response, where ExpandedNameOffset points to an empty WCHAR string (\x00\x00), flows through PktExpandSpecialEntryFromReferral() unchecked, the kernel dereferences a bad pointer, and the machine BSODs. Corelight reproduced the crash 11/11 times on Server 2022 and 3/3 times on Server 2019.
- The attack chain requires only network adjacency and abuses the implicit trust Windows places in DFS referral responses. The attacker stands up a rogue SMB server, coerces the target to initiate an SMB connection toward it using existing public tooling, then replies with the malformed DFS_REFERRAL_V3 payload. mup.sys processes the response, faults, and the server reboots. The entire exchange takes seconds, and because an attacker in this position can repeat it continuously, they can keep Domain Controllers or other critical servers offline indefinitely.
- On the victim host, the crash leaves almost nothing useful. Event ID 41 (kernel power) and Event ID 6008 (unexpected shutdown) appear in the System log, but no minidump and no clear crash reason. The server does not get a chance to log anything about why it faulted. This makes network-side evidence the primary forensic source.
- Zeek's conn.log provides the post-crash signal. When mup.sys null-dereferences, the TCP stack dies instantly, leaving established sessions silent. Zeek records these as conn_state=S1. After the server recovers, other hosts attempting to resume connections receive RSTs from a machine with no session state. Depending on timing relative to Zeek's default 5-minute inactivity timeout, those appear as conn_state=RSTR (reboot within the timeout) or conn_state=RSTRH (RST arrives as a new mid-stream connection with no SYN, after the timeout). A sudden cluster of S1, RSTR, and RSTRH connections all involving the same server is a hunt-worthy pattern for unexpected reboots, including exploitation of this vulnerability.
Practitioner takeaway: network logging is the detection path here, not host logs. Hunt your Zeek conn.log for a burst of conn_state values of S1, RSTR, and RSTRH from the same server within a short window, especially if that server is a Domain Controller, then cross-reference with Event ID 41 and Event ID 6008 in the Windows System log to confirm an unexpected reboot. Because the malformed DFS response is application-layer content inside otherwise normal-looking SMB traffic, connection metadata alone will not catch it: you need full transaction logging to see the malformed DFS_REFERRAL_V3 payload. Patch priority is Windows Server 2019, 2022, and 2025 via the October 2026 cumulative update.
